item.title: Wan'Dale Robinson out for season with ankle injury
item.description: The Titans will not have one of their key receivers for the rest of 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The Titans will not have one of their key receivers for the rest of 2026.

Receiver Wan'Dale Robinson is out for the season after being placed on injured reserve this week with an ankle injury, head coach Robert Saleh told reporters in his Wednesday press conference.

Robinson signed with the Titans as a free agent in the offseason, reuniting him with former Giants head coach Brian Daboll, who serves as Tennessee’s offensive coordinator.

In nine games with three starts this season, Robinson caught 38 passes for 272 yards with three touchdowns.

item.title: NFL news, live updates: Aidan Hutchinson reportedly suffers torn ACL on sack celebration; Patriots QB Drake Maye out indefinitely with ankle injury
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news coming out of Week 10.
item.content:encoded:
Another NFL Sunday is in the books, with just one game left in Week 10 as the Baltimore Ravens host the LA Chargers on "Monday Night Football."

Sunday kicked off with a bang as the Detroit Lions and New England Patriots faced off in Munich, Germany, with injuries to two stars that will have all eyes drawn as the new week plays out. Lions star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson suffered what is feared to be a season-ending ACL tear while celebrating a sack against Patriots quarterback Drake Maye … who suffered an ankle injury on that very sack, which knocked him out of the game and could cost him the season.

Week 10 also offered us our first look at Las Vegas Raiders No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza as a starter. He led scoring drives on each of the Raiders' first two possessions and entered halftime with a 10-7 lead over the Seattle Seahawks, but Drew Lock rallied with two passing touchdowns in the third quarter to take the lead, improving to 3-0 as a starter for Seattle this season. Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers exited the loss with an ankle injury.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more coming out of Week 10.

item.title: Eagles to start Joe Milton in Week 11 against the Steelers
item.description: It will be Milton's second career start.
item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni confirmed that Joe Milton III will make his second start of the season on Sunday against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Milton is the third starting QB that Philadelphia has used this season. Starting quarterback Jalen Hurts remains sidelined indefinitely with blood clots in his lungs. Tanner McKee stepped into the starting role, but after going 0-3, Sirianni pivoted to Milton, whom Philadelphia signed off the Dallas Cowboys' practice squad.

In his first career start against the Giants, Milton finished 18 of 34 passing for 169 yards. He also added 64 yards on nine carries, but his effort wasn't enough to keep the Eagles from losing 19-11. Milton also lost a fumble.

While Milton didn't play well, neither did anyone else on the Eagles. Saquon Barkley found the end zone for a touchdown, but finished with 22 yards on 13 carries. Philly didn't have DeVonta Smith in the passing game, and rookie Makai Lemon finished with 61 yards on six receptions.

Tight end Dallas Goedert had 50 yards on five receptions. No other Philadelphia player had more than 25 receiving yards or three receptions. The Eagles desperately need a more consistent offense, and Sirianni is giving Milton another chance this weekend to deliver.

Philadelphia started the season with close wins over the Washington Commanders and the Tennessee Titans. After that, though, the season has taken a sharp downward turn. Key injuries to the offense are easy to blame, but the Eagles head into this weekend's matchup against Pittsburgh on a seven-game losing streak.

The Eagles are in last place and desperately need a win. Pittsburgh comes into this game coming off a loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. The Steelers are 6-3 and in second place in the AFC North, trailing the Bengals by one game.

item.title: Carnell Tate injury update: Titans rookie WR will practice today
item.description: Some good injury updates for the Titans today
item.content:encoded:
Carnell Tate has missed the Tennessee Titans’ last two games with a shoulder injury he suffered in the loss to the Cleveland Browns. Robert Saleh said today that the rookie wide receiver will practice today. It sounds like he has a good chance to be back for the game against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday.

Tate has been really good this season with 34 catches for 413 yards and a touchdown through 7 games.

Saleh also said that Anthony Hill and Cody Barton will return to practice today. It will be interesting to see what that means for Cedric Gray. For reasons that aren’t exactly clear, Gray spent most of his time on the sideline when both Hill and Barton were healthy. Gray, who might be the best defender left with Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker both gone, was really good last week against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

In addition to getting those guys back on the practice field, Fernando Carmona will get his first practice in since he injured his ankle against the New York Giants.

Saleh also said that Wan’Dale Robinson will miss the rest of the season. The team placed him on IR yesterday.

item.title: Patrick Mahomes found his deep ball again in Chiefs’ latest win
item.description: Mahomes and Kansas City unleashed the deep ball against Atlanta on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Atlanta Falcons35-13 on Sunday to improve to 7-2 and tie the Denver Broncos for first place in the AFC West.

The Chiefs offense suffered multiple big blows from injuries before and during the game, but they made up for it with their passing attack.

Quarterback Patrick Mahomes had a massive day, throwing for 348 yards on 22 completions, a 135.4 quarterback rating, and a whopping five touchdowns, the most he has thrown in a game since his most recent MVP season in 2022.

Mahomes’ monster day came from an onslaught of deep balls, multiple new weapons in the offense and well-timed protection sets from the offensive line.

A week after Chiefs fans held their breath when he exited the field with a visible elbow injury, Mahomes played his best game of the season and instilled a reinvented attack.

Connecting with Downs

Josh Downs played only eight snaps on passing downs, but he made the most of them, and Mahomes made sure to find him.

On four catches in five targets, he put up 53 yards and a touchdown, showing the route-tree diversity the Chiefs coveted when they acquired him.

With a play-action look and an expanded pocket for Mahomes, Caliendo pulls, the middle of the field opens up for Downs, and Mahomes finds him for a 20+ yard gain.

This look is as easy a layup as there is for Mahomes, and it was a great way to get Downs involved in a play that helped the offense move the chains.

Later in the first half, Mahomes would find Downs for the pair’s first touchdown connection.

The Chiefs sought a man-beating wideout before the deadline, and that is what they got in Downs.

Out of a tight bunch, the Chiefs go with a post-wheel concept, with Downs releasing all the way from the inside. The deep safety follows Xavier Worthy on the post; meanwhile, Downs already has a space advantage on the corner due to his delayed release behind Worthy and Cyrus Allen.

The corner squares up Downs, who slow plays it initially, but once he recognizes the safety go to the post, he plants and gets upfield in a hurry.

Mahomes maneuvers the pocket and delivers a perfect back shoulder throw.

The pocket isn’t perfect, but with the front line walled off and the edge rushers running past him, he has time to step up and fire a bullet.

Downs’ role will only grow in the coming weeks.

Shots for Armstrong and Allen

Downs wasn’t the only Chiefs wideout to find the endzone on Sunday.

Mahomes connected with two of his newer wide receivers on big shots to the end zone, the first to Cyrus Allen.

This play is a simple concept being run to a high level, and Allen runs a fantastic route to find the endzone.

Only three Chiefs run routes on the play, but the stop-and-start move from Allen, Mahomes holds the safety to the middle with his eyes before firing it deep.

With seven in protection, Mahomes has plenty of time to drop back and fires a dart to Allen, who easily took it in for six.

Not every concept needs to be a complex equation; sometimes the best course is to let good players win snaps.

Later in the game, Mahomes found Armstrong deep on a third down.

On third down and one, the Chiefs run a roll-out look with receivers flooding one side of the field. Mahomes has time to throw shorter routes and convert the needed yard, but Armstrong has his man beat deep, and Mahomes knows it.

With a little pump fake of his own, Mahomes holds the defensive end in place and buys time to roll and throw the ball deep. With a big rip, Mahomes fires the pass, and Armstrong locates it in the air and comes back to it.

Mahomes lets it fly, and Armstrong is there to haul it in, likely securing himself more snaps and more targets moving forward.

Finding Rice

Rashee Rice didn’t find the end zone, but he led the Chiefs with 82 receiving yards on five receptions.

Early in the game, Mahomes and Rice connected on their usual underneath looks, with Mahomes doing a great job to extend the pocket.

These underneath throws have been the bread and butter for the Mahomes and Rice connection, but later in the game, Mahomes would finally give Rice a chance to show off his ball-tracking ability.

Rice and Allen line up out of a stacked look, and on the snap both run vertical routes, with Allen going up the middle and Rice staying outside. The deep safeties go after Allen, but with leverage inside, Rice continues upfield vertically.

In the pocket, Mahomes has to deal with pressure and can’t even fully step into the pass, and it doesn’t matter.

With a flick of the wrist, Mahomes throws a bomb, and Rice does a phenomenal job tracking the ball and hauling it in for a big catch.

Most of Mahomes and Rice’s big plays have come underneath and with YAC attached, so it will be interesting to see if the deep ball connections continue.

The bottom line

Mahomes must have heard the ADOT (Average Depth of Target) crowd this week, and he made it his mission to attack the Falcons vertically. This performance also came as he missed his starting right tackle and starting running back; right guard Trey Smith left the game with a concussion, and center Creed Humphrey missed snaps after being gouged in the eye.

Mahomes is as good as ever, and while it is still to be seen if the deep ball can become a consistent threat in the Chiefs’ offense, the building blocks are now in place, and the chemistry between Mahomes and his receivers is coming into its own.

item.title: Chicago Bears 1-on-1: Can Theo Benedet neutralize the Saints’ Chase Young?
item.description: The Bears enter Sunday as heavy favorites against the Saints. That doesn’t mean Theo Benedet won’t have his hands full.
item.content:encoded:
On paper, the New Orleans Saints might be the worst team the Chicago Bears have faced since Week 4 against the New York Jets. The Saints rank 15th in the league in scoring offense at 22.4 points per game. They are 25th in the league in scoring defense at 26.2 ppg allowed.

They are an average to below-average team, but they might yet surprise the Bears.

The Saints still have a lot to play for, despite their 3-6 record. They remain only one game back in the paltry NFC South, and remain in the upswing of a franchise rebuild eager to get a taste of the postseason.

Their star player right now is WR Chris Olave, who is 8th in the NFL with 764 receiving yards. He has turned into a true WR1 in his age 26 season.

If after Chris Olave you are struggling to name many Saints players, that’s understandable. Their roster is young and lacking in top-end talent. But there is something lurking beneath the surface that the Bears need to take very seriously.

New Orleans has two of the top four sack leaders in the NFL right now, with DE Carl Granderson boasting 8.5 sacks and his foil Chase Young sporting 8 sacks. 16.5 sacks between two players 9 games into a season is not a coincidence.

While Granderson may have the higher count presently, he typically lines up on the right side and will face Darnell Wright, who is… really freaking good. It’s no given, but I think that Wright should be able to hold his own.

On the other side, though, is the far more interesting matchup. Chase Young, the revived 2nd overall pick in the 2020 draft, has found a new home in New Orleans and has really turned into one of the premier pass-rushers in the league. He gets the opportunity to line up on the Bears left side, which will likely be manned by Theo Benedet.

Benedet is hitting a stride himself and holds the 3rd best OT pass blocking win rate in the league entering Week 11 at 92%. He has earned the right to start at LT until Ozzy Trapilo can prove himself to be healthy enough to play like he did in 2025.

Still, Chase Young’s physicality is elite. Just look at what he did against highly touted rookie Spencer Fano.

Benedet, as we know, was not a high-end draft pick. And while he has improved drastically in his third season with the Bears, he will have his hands full going up against Young. If the Bears are to win on Sunday, devising a plan to help Benedet will be crucial. It will also be important for Theo to step up and win 1-on-1s when his number is called.

item.title: Cowboys have the perfect chance to bounce back against Tennessee
item.description: How optimistic are you for this week?
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys dropped to 4-6 after a wild 46-40 loss to San Francisco, but Sunday brings a much more favorable matchup. Tennessee comes to Dallas at 1-8, having lost its last three games and allowed 40-plus points in consecutive weeks. The defense struggled badly against San Francisco, forcing a desperate comeback that fell short.

Dak Prescott now has 2,724 yards and 21 touchdown passes this season. Tennessee has allowed 43 points to Cincinnati and 40 to Jacksonville in its last two games. This looks like another opportunity for Prescott and the offense to score heavily, especially after what George Pickens did against the 49ers. 

Pickens returned against San Francisco and immediately produced his best game of the season. He caught three touchdowns and finished with 145 receiving yards. Now Tennessee has to deal with Pickens alongside CeeDee Lamb, who already has 976 receiving yards and eight touchdowns. The Titans simply don’t have one receiver they can concentrate on stopping.

The numbers between these two team’s offenses aren’t close. Dallas averages 28 points per game, fifth in the NFL. Tennessee averages only 18, ranking 28th. The Cowboys also average 368 yards per game compared with Tennessee’s 278. If Dallas gets into the high 20s or 30s again, Tennessee may struggle to keep pace. This is where having both Lamb and Pickens, along with players like Ryan Flournoy will come into play. 

Perhaps the most interesting statistic is time of possession. The Titans average only 25:12 with the football, worst in the NFL. That gives Dallas exactly what it needs after watching San Francisco control huge parts of Sunday’s game. Get Tennessee off the field and give Prescott, Lamb and Pickens as many possessions as possible.

Tennessee has some serious injury issues and placed starting guard Peter Skoronski on injured reserve because of a hamstring injury. Linebackers Anthony Hill Jr. and Cody Barton are dealing with injury, and wide receiver Carnell Tate has a big question mark on whether he’ll suit up this Sunday. Wan’Dale Robinson is going on injured reserve.

The offensive line injuries should interest a Dallas pass rush that finally produced some numbers against San Francisco. They recorded five sacks against Brock Purdy, including four in the first half. Cam Ward is a talented young quarterback, but Dallas needs to make him uncomfortable behind a weakened offensive line. Tennessee’s rookie quarterback can be pressured into mistakes Ward has shown improvement, but he is still learning.

Through nine games he has thrown eight touchdowns and six interceptions with an 80.7 passer rating. He threw another interception against Jacksonville on Sunday.

Then there’s the past between these two teams. The Cowboys won the last time these teams met when they travelled to Tennessee in December 2022, coming away with a 27-13 victory. Now the Titans have to travel to AT&T Stadium while carrying one of the worst records in football and knowing they’ve lost four out of the last six meetings between these two teams.

item.title: Titans place WR Wan'Dale Robinson on season-ending IR due to ankle injury, sign Xavier Restrepo to active roster
item.description: Robinson currently leads the Titans with three receiving TDs.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans are adding wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson to injured reserve due to an ankle injury, per team reporter Jim Wyatt. Head coach Robert Saleh said that it will be season-ending.

In a corresponding move, the team is signing wide receiver Xavier Restrepo to the active roster.

Robinson suffered the ankle injury in the team's Week 10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars and could not return to the game. Restrepo was activated from the practice squad on game day and finished with 31 yards on three receptions.

Restrepo may be a familiar name to college football fans. He played for the University of Miami through the 2024 season, his final year with Cam Ward at quarterback. He finished that year with 1,127 yards and 11 touchdowns.

Restrepo hasn't held onto an active roster spot until now, but his former rapport with Ward may help the Titans offense get on the same page and into a groove.

Robinson is in his first year with the Titans after signing a 4-year, $70 million deal this offseason. He has been in the mix for the team's top wide receiver along with rookie Carnell Tate and Elic Ayomanor.

Robinson has played in all nine games for Tennessee this season. He has brought in 38 receptions for 272 yards and a team-high three receiving touchdowns.

Tennessee will take on the Dallas Cowboys this week. Tate was back at practice on Wednesday, so there is hope he will be active for the game. Otherwise, Ward will lean on Ayomanor, Chimere Dike and Restrepo as his top wideouts.

item.title: Why a franchise tag may not work for Puka Nacua
item.description: Can the Rams even afford a franchise tag for Nacua?
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams have had a decision to make with Puka Nacua since the beginning of the 2026 offseason, and the longer they hold off on his next contract, the more likely it becomes that the fourth-year receiver won’t get one from Les Snead and Sean McVay. Nacua is set to become a 2027 free agent and ESPN’s Dan Graziano speculated on Wednesday that the Rams could be too concerned with his off-field issues and/or his injury to commit to him like other teams have committed to number one receivers.

Nacua didn’t get the big contract extension that Jaxon Smith-Njigba got last offseason, even though he was eligible. And the Rams don’t hold a fifth-year option on him for next year because he wasn’t a first-round pick. Nacua also made bad headlines with his off-field behavior in the offseason and could still face league discipline under the personal conduct policy.

Plus, he’s banged up again. He missed two games earlier this season with hip and groin injuries, and he’s currently on IR with a knee injury that will cost him at least four more games (counting the one he missed Sunday) and possibly more than that. Nacua played all 17 games in his rookie season but hasn’t managed to do that since. He’s 25 years old and a brilliant player, but his play style makes you wonder about his longevity. All of that is to say: I could at least imagine a scenario in which the Rams let him hit free agency, or franchise him and listen to offers.

Graziano didn’t get into the weeds of what a franchise tag would look like and how challenging that would be for the Rams given their slate of free agents in 2027.

What does a WR tag cost?

OvertheCap.com is projecting a $30.9 million franchise tag for wide receivers in 2027.

What that Means:

  • The Rams would have to pay Nacua a fully-guaranteed $30.9 million salary in 2027
  • The Rams would have a deadline to either extend Nacua, pay him the tag, or rescind the tag
  • The non-exclusive tag means Nacua could negotiate with other teams and if he signs with a team and the Rams don’t match the offer, the Rams would get two first-round picks from that team
  • The exclusive tag means Nacua can’t negotiate with other teams
  • The Rams could still trade Nacua to another team on the exclusive tag
  • The Rams could still extend Nacua before the deadline, this would just buy them some time

Paying Nacua a $30.9 million salary in 2027 seems exceptionally challenging for L.A..

The Rams only have one starting offensive lineman under contract — AJ Jackson — and only one recent draft pick who might be a contender to start — Keagen Trost — meaning that at best L.A. only has three starting offensive line positions to fill. They will have a hard time replacing anyone in the draft because the Rams don’t have a first-round pick and they’re not keen on starting rookies anyway.

The Rams also have to make a decision on WR2, as Davante Adams is a free agent.

There are plenty of other free agents, including Kobie Turner, Byron Young, and Ethan Evans. In fact, the Rams also need to pick a kicker and potentially invest more money in special teams next year.

An extension for Nacua could carry a 2027 cap hit of roughly $10-$15 million. That makes a tag 2-3 times more expensive next year at a time when the Rams have to sign almost half of their important starters. A tag would be very difficult for the Rams to pull off.

Will Nacua be a free agent?

I highly doubt it. The Rams would only get a third-round comp pick in 2028 if Nacua leaves in free agency. That’s not enough compensation for one of the NFL’s best players who is only going to be 26. It would be a mistake of absurd proportions.

The Rams will figure something out with Nacua, most likely. Free agency is highly unlikely. But the longer the Rams make us speculate, the more speculation that will occur.

item.title: Titans designate Fernando Carmona to return from IR
item.description: Offensive line reinforcements are on the way
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans have opened the practice window for rookie guard Fernando Carmona to return from injured reserve. Carmona was injured in the Titans’ 12-7 loss to the New York Giants in Week 3. He started the first three games of the season at right guard. The Titans will now have 21 days to activate Carmona.

Carmona, a 5th-round pick out of Arkansas in the 2026 NFL Draft, was one of the biggest stories of training camp. He came in and won the starting job with a great camp.

Jackson Slater, Carmona’s backup, was also injured in that game. The offensive line has done a remarkable job with both of those guys out of the lineup. A lot of credit goes to offensive line coach Carmen Bricillo. He has done a great job getting the next guy up ready to play each week.

It cannot be overstated how important having a good offensive line coach is. It will allow the Titans to not have to invest high picks in interior offensive linemen.

item.title: Colts CB Justin Walley named the AFC defensive player of the week
item.description: The Colts ended a five-game losing streak with last Sunday's win over the Dolphins and a defensive touchdown played a big role in the 24-22 win.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts ended a five-game losing streak with last Sunday's win over the Dolphins and a defensive touchdown played a big role in the 24-22 win.

Cornerback Justin Walley got home on a blitz deep inside Miami territory and separated Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord from the ball. Defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore recovered the ball for a touchdown.

Walley had five tackles, two tackles for loss and two passes defensed overall in the win. The third-round pick has 40 tackles, two sacks and three forced fumbles to this point in his rookie season.

The NFL named Walley the AFC defensive player of the week on Wednesday. It's the first time a Colt has won the award since early in the 2024 season.

item.title: Why is Luke Butkus exempt from public criticism?
item.description: Matt LaFleur refuses to offer any kind of pointed criticism for his offensive line coach.
item.content:encoded:
Matt LaFleur has no problem criticizing the offensive line. He has no problems saying there are issues with how the offensive line is coached. He, like everyone else, knows the offensive line is a problem.

So why is his offensive line coach exempt from criticism? Bring up the name Luke Butkus and suddenly the offensive line picture is rosy.

“He was the same guy when we were rolling,” LaFleur said of Butkus after the Packers’ latest offensive line collapse. “I think it’s easy to pinpoint and point the finger, and everybody wants to pinpoint blame, but the blame can go to everybody. So it’s all of us in this together. Certainly it starts with myself, and then it goes to everybody else, and it’s coaches and players collectively.”

According to LaFleur, then, it’s not Butkus’s fault, but it also is his fault, and it’s the players’ fault, and it’s the other coaches’ fault, and possibly the general manager’s fault. It might also be your fault, which is something I hadn’t considered before. I’ve been spending Packers’ gamedays just watching their offensive line get shredded and never once have I tried to do anything about it. I’m sorry. It starts with me.

But why can’t Butkus be criticized? Why is it impossible that he’s part of the problem?

I understand that LaFleur isn’t going to stand at the lectern and blast one of his coaches any more than he’s going to single out an individual player for post-loss criticism delivered through the media, but it’s insulting to our collective football intelligence that he won’t even entertain the question.

That’s not hyperbole, lest we forget. After an embarrassing Thursday Night Football loss to the Atlanta Falcons earlier this year, reporters brought Luke Butkus up as a possible reason for the poor offensive line performance. LaFleur said “I’m not even going to respond to that.”

Why? LaFleur is more than willing to criticize the coaching obliquely.

After the Packers’ Week 1 collapse LaFleur said he and the Packers’ coaching staff have “got to find a way to get it done” regardless of who’s on the field.

A few days after the Falcons loss, LaFleur directly criticized the offensive line’s fundamentals.

“II think that’s where the majority of our focus will lie is in terms of our pass sets and how we’re passing off twists, how we punch,” he said. “All that stuff, it’s got to improve in a hurry.”

That’s a particularly telling bit of criticism, because Butkus himself has identified improving fundamentals as one of the core aspects of his job. In 2025, Butkus was asked specifically what Jordan Morgan needed to improve to earn a full-time starting job, and Butkus responded that it was all about fundamentals — which he and the other coaches would work to help him improve.

“So you’d better be good at technique, and that’s what we have to do constantly, be fanatics about working your technique and making sure if you’re letting defenders in your chest, you better be better with your hands,” Butkus said. “And that’s our job as coaches, help him with that.”

Previous linemen have praised Butkus and offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich for helping them improve their fundamentals. The most pointed praise came from former Packers guard Jon Runyan.

“Coach Steno, Coach Butkus, they make it so simple and it’s so easy to understand so that we go out there, we take everything they tell us from the film room onto the field and it’s just really easy to follow,” he said in 2021. “They just do a really good job of holding all of us to a really high standard and making sure that we know our stuff and they feel comfortable. They’re just doing their job at such a high level, it makes it a lot easier for us.”

Why, then, are there repeated questions and concerns from the head coach about the offensive line’s fundamentals?

It seems telling that the Runyan quote comes from 2021, when Adam Stenavich was a full-time offensive line coach and Butkus was merely his assistant. Both have been promoted since then; in 2022, Stenavich made the jump to offensive coordinator, while Butkus got the promotion to offensive line coach. Since then, it doesn’t seem like hyperbole to say the offensive line has been in a steady state of decline.

Personnel plays a role in that; the Packers’ line is certainly less talented now than it was in the early Matt LaFleur era. But a coach’s job is to work with what he’s got, and many of the Packers’ early season struggles centered on Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk, two players who had been in the Packers’ system for years. Both had several seasons of development under their belt, tutored all the while by Luke Butkus. If they weren’t ready to go when finally called upon, who’s to blame other than their position coach?

The near-automatic response to LaFleur’s reticence to move on from struggling coaches is loyalty, but I’m not sure where that comes from in this particular instance. LaFleur and Stenavich go way back; Stenavich first worked with LaFleur as a practice squad member of the Houston Texans while LaFleur was a low-level assistant on Gary Kubiak’s staff. But there’s no such connection with Luke Butkus. He arrived courtesy of Nathaniel Hackett, with whom he’d worked for the Jacksonville Jaguars. His relationship with LaFleur began in 2019; it’s not like there’s some deep-seated relationship there.

Maybe it’s just LaFleur’s general hesitance toward firing anyone rearing its head. Maybe there’s more going on behind the scenes than we’re seeing publicly. Maybe the second this season ends, Butkus will be out of a job.

But for now, it seems like the man that should be getting rightly criticized — and in some cases, actually is facing some not-so-veiled criticism — is viewed as untouchable. In a season on the brink of total collapse, that’s hard to understand.

item.title: Jaelan Phillips wins first NFC defensive player of the week award
item.description: The Panthers moved into sole possession of first place in the NFC South with their victory over the Saints on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Panthers moved into sole possession of first place in the NFC South with their victory over the Saints on Sunday.

Now one of their players has been recognized for his performance in the win.

Edge rusher Jaelan Phillips has been named NFC defensive player of the week.

Phillips had five total tackles with three for loss, a sack, and a fumble recovery that led to a Panthers touchdown in the 20-17 victory.

According to the league, Phillips is the second player in the conference to have three TFLs and a fumble recovery in a single game in 2026.

This is Phillips’ first career defensive player of the week award.

In his first season with Carolina, Phillips has tallied 3.5 sacks, five tackles for loss, and eight QB hits so far in 2026.

item.title: Joe Burrow named AFC offensive player of the week for second time this season
item.description: Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is the betting favorite to be the NFL MVP this season and games like the one he had last Sunday are the reason why he's in that spot.
item.content:encoded:
Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is the betting favorite to be the NFL MVP this season and games like the one he had last Sunday are the reason why he's in that spot.

Burrow lit up the Steelers during a 38-18 win that extended Cincinnati's winning streak to five games. Burrow was 35-of-44 for 409 yards and four touchdowns in the victory.

The four touchdowns moved him up to 20 over the course of the winning streak and he leads the league with 27 touchdown passes over the entire season.

The NFL announced on Wednesday that Burrow has been named the AFC offensive player of the week. It's the second time he's won that prize this season and the 10th time in his career.

item.title: Predicting how the NFC North will finish with 4 great teams
item.description: Four brilliant teams, but only one can win.
item.content:encoded:
It’s a really bad year to be a good team in the NFC North. While the majority of the NFL’s divisions have settled into a football bell curve of the good, fine, and bad — the North is stacked with four of the league’s best teams fighting over three playoff spots down the stretch. Someone is going to win, cementing themselves as a true contender in the NFC, two teams will likely secure wild-card spots, becoming the most dangerous non-winners in the playoffs, and one team is going to finish with a 10+ win record and have nothing to show for it.

We’re hurtling towards another season where one fanbase decries the NFL’s playoff format. The only question that remains is: Who? The Bears, Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have incredible characteristics in their own right, but diving into trends, remaining schedule, and future potential, there’s a likely way we’re going to see this play out.

Chicago Bears

Current record: 7-2
Remaining SoS (lower is better): +14.7
Future opponents: Saints, Lions, Jaguars, Dolphins, Bills, Packers, Lions, Vikings
Projected finish: 12-5

The Bears are so much fun to watch. Boasting a Top 10 offense and defense in scoring/scoring allowed, the complete revitalization of this football team by Ben Johnson is almost complete in just his second year at the helm.

Caleb Williams took another step forward in his development this season, though it hasn’t always been perfect. A hamstring injury forced him to miss three games, and his overall performance has been excellent on paper, but there’s a key element to his game that’s still missing: Red Zone efficiency. Moving the football between the 20s hasn’t been a problem for Williams this season, but it’s clear that Johnson still doesn’t fully trust his young QB in short-field situations, favoring a shift to the run game over asking him to make tight throws.

This has resulted in him being on pace for an injury-adjusted 23 passing touchdowns this season, which puts him around 16th in the NFL in passing TDs, much closer to the Bo Nix/Geno Smith caliber of QB than the league’s elite. Bears fans shouldn’t take this as a knock on Williams, but rather an exciting development for the future. We are still yet to see Caleb be fully unlocked, and he’s already on pace to lead this team to the playoffs. I have no doubt the Bears coaching staff can round out his game and make him even better.

When it comes to the remaining schedule, the Bears boast the toughest remaining slate in the NFC North. They have enough ability to win the majority of their remaining games, but not quite enough to take the division outright. The x-factor down the stretch will be Jeffrey Simmons. One of the best acquisitions around the trade deadline, Chicago got a massive boost to their defense with the interior pass rusher, who has been fantastic since his arrival. If Simmons is capable of disrupting key drives then there’s a real chance the Bears could flip another loss to a win down the stretch.

Detroit Lions

Current record: 7-2
Remaining SoS (lower is better): +2.8
Future opponents: Buccaneers, Bears, Falcons, Titans, Vikings, Giants, Bears, Packers
Projected finish: 13-4

“Undeniable” is the best adjective for the Lions offense this season. Working off the inverse of most offensive principles, Detroit uses Jared Goff as their chain-mover and red zone scoring threat, while Jahmyr Gibbs’ rushing ability delivers the explosive plays. This has been incredibly difficult for opponents to deal with, as the Lions are poised to be the only team in the NFL to finish with a QB over 4,500 yards passing and a running back with over 1,500 yards rushing,

If you can sense the “but” coming, you’d be right. Detroit’s offense has been incredible, but the defense is another story entirely. The injury bug has bitten this team big time, with its two most important players all out for the remainder of the season in LB Jack Campbell, and now DE Aidan Hutchinson, who hurt himself in Week 10.

Before these injuries, a banged-up secondary was struggling, meaning things are only going to get worse for Detroit defensively from here. This team ranks 15th in the NFL in points allowed and 28th against the pass. These are scary metrics for a team poised to hit the playoffs and face some of the league’s best quarterbacks. The saving grace here is that the remaining schedule looks great for them, with only the Vikings and Bears looking like real challenges at this point.

This is a team that will get a high wild card seed, likely win a playoff game, but major questions remain about whether their defense has enough to stop the best teams in the league.

Green Bay Packers

Current record: 6-4
Remaining SoS (lower is better): +12.0
Future opponents: Rams, Saints, Bills, Dolphins, Bears, Texans, Lions
Projected finish: 10-7

It’s been a weird year for the Green Bay Packers. Full of ups and downs, the Packers have shown they can rise to beat some of the NFL’s best teams, but also lose inexplicably to the likes of the Falcons, and be pushed to overtime by the Jets. This leaves us with a team that is very good, but just feels a step behind everyone else in the NFC North right now.

Jordan Love and the Packers’ passing game are fascinatingly weird. This is a unit that never makes things easy on themselves, opting to generate as many explosive deep passes through the air as possible, in a very feast-or-famine playstyle. At times this has been incredible, typified by their blowout win over the Bears in Week 5 — but also looked sophomoric and unsophisticated against the Vikings in Week 10.

When we get down to brass tacks, there are just too many points of failure for Green Bay this season. The running game has been atrocious, the defense has been middling, and above all else it’s tough to discern what the identity of this football team is. They’re good at a lot of things, but not great at anything in particular. That’s ultimately what will put them on the outside looking in when the playoffs roll around, especially in light of a difficult schedule down the stretch.

Minnesota Vikings

Current record: 7-2
Remaining SoS (lower is better): -5.9
Future opponents: 49ers, Falcons, Panthers, Patriots, Lions, Commanders, Jets, Bears
Projected finish: 14-3

It’s impossible to heap any more praise on the Minnesota defense. Watch this team play one game and you immediately understand how special this unit is. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores has steadily improved his players from the moment he arrived, with 2026 being the crescendo of his brilliance — orchestrating a group of guys who aren’t household names, and transforming them into a group of monsters.

There have been some standout performances in Dallas Turner and Andrew Van Ginkel, but overall this isn’t a team you’d characterize as being full of elite talent on defense. The only thing holding them back was an absolutely putrid offense, which was led by two horrible quarterbacks in Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz.

That all changed at the NFL trade deadline when the Vikings re-acquired Kirk Cousins for their playoff push. The impact was immediately noticeable, with Cousins being simply good enough to allow the defense to swallow the Packers, and ultimately deliver the win.

Minnesota is in an incredible spot right now where they not only have momentum behind them, but the easiest remaining schedule in the NFC North. The only game they’re not favored in to close out the season is against the 49ers, which could quite easily be a win, depending on how the defense is able to stop Brock Purdy’s quick passing game.

It’s beginning to feel like the Vikings’ division to lose, with the stars aligning for them. As for the playoffs? We’ll need to wait and see. As brilliant as this team could be, there’s also a weight of baggage and history pressuring them to perform. It’s unclear if this team is ready to rise to the moment.

item.title: Commanders LB Sonny Styles’ processing power makes him more dangerous
item.description: Sonny Styles has proven to be a centerpiece for the Commanders defense over the short- and long-term
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants faced a third-and-3 coming out of the two-minute warning, needing to move the sticks to maintain a slim lead and possession of the ball.  

Commanders linebacker Sonny Styles understood that situation. His quarterback had thrown interceptions on consecutive series leading up to this moment, and Washington needed to give Jayden Daniels one more shot to go win it.  

The stakes didn’t change Styles’ approach to crucial play. The Ohio State product diagnosed it appropriately, sensed what was coming and used freak athleticism to make the defensive play of the day. 

“Last time we played them and we had a third-and-4 situation around midfield and they had a crack toss to the back,” Styles said. “When they went empty, just looking at the tight end, it looked like he was cracking. Charles said something like that, too, so I thought it was going to be a QB run. I just reacted.” 

He reacted well in a play you’ve certainly seen a bunch by now.  

“Everyone understood that we had to get a stop right there,” Styles said. “Guys bowed up.” 

Washington got the ball back and Daniels rewarded that effort with a decisive, 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs. That play will lead the highlights from a 24-21 victory over the Giants that essentially saved Washington’s season.  

None of that happens without Styles and an overall defensive effort where Washington’s foot never left the gas.  

This wasn’t a singular event. The No. 7 overall NFL draft pick has been a marvel in this early season, and not solely due to insane athleticism. He’s a smart player who can read offenses well and make plays on the ball. While he’s far from perfect and with room for improvement, his first nine game qualify as an excellent start to his NFL career.  

Styles has 80 tackles and the season’s just nine games deep. While number of tackles isn’t the important stat that it used to be, that’s still a sign that Styles is doing things right. Jeremy Reaves’ 55 is the next highest total on Washington’s defense. The rookie, Styles, has had 13 tackles in four of the past five games.  

He has validated GM Adam Peters’ decision to draft a non-premium position at No. 7.  

The dude can play.  

Styles was critical of some plays, including some hesitance as a blitzer, which is keeping him a step behind.  

His stat line, overall: 80 tackles, including five for a loss, a sack, and interception, four passes defensed and four quarterback pressures in 46 blitzes. He has allowed 30 catches for 288 yards and a touchdown on 45 targets, for an 82.5 passer rating allowed. 

The Commanders will need him leading the defensive surge toward the better play and consistent wins that are required for a real turnaround. The scary part about Styles is that his athleticism will get more effective as he takes more snaps and processes information faster.  

He’s the primary reason for hope and the long-term success on defense, assuming, of course, that the front office can surround him with talent in ways they haven’t quite done for Daniels.  

That’s a discussion for the offseason. Styles and the Commanders will continue competing for the NFC East title down the stretch, with that Week 10 win against the Giants as a possible pivot point.

“This win isn’t going to turn the whole season,” Styles said. “We have to keep working, keep pushing and get getting better.”

item.title: Seahawks re-sign Deven Eastern to practice squad
item.description: The team’s seventh-round pick was waived off the active roster on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
A member of the Seattle Seahawks’ 2026 draft class is back, again.

After being waived to begin the week, the Seahawks signed seventh-round pick Deven Eastern to their practice squad on Tuesday, the team announced.

Eastern, selected with the team’s penultimate selection in this year’s draft, 242nd overall, has spent most of the season on Seattle’s practice squad after he was waived during the cut down from 90 to 53.

Promoted to the active roster ahead of the Week 9 win over the Arizona Cardinals, as the Seahawks entered the game without Leonard Williams or Brandon Pili, Eastern was waived from the 53-man roster on Monday.

Despite spending two weeks on the active roster, Eastern did not get on the field on defense in Week 9 and was inactive for Seattle’s Week 10 win in Las Vegas.

In a corresponding move, the Seahawks released quarterback and former UFL MVP Adrian Martinez from the practice squad, in the latest sign they expect Sam Darnold to be back in the fold as they emerge from their bye week.

item.title: Christian Parker loses play-calling as Cowboys’ defensive coordinator
item.description: Back on October 13, we noted how Christian Parker seemed to be getting Sean Desai’d with the Dallas Cowboys bringing Mike Pettine in as a defensive assistant. That prophecy has now fully come to fruition with Parker losing play-calling duty to Pettine. It’s not hard to understand why the Cowboys are making this move; Dallas […]
item.content:encoded:
Back on October 13, we noted how Christian Parker seemed to be getting Sean Desai’d with the Dallas Cowboys bringing Mike Pettine in as a defensive assistant. That prophecy has now fully come to fruition with Parker losing play-calling duty to Pettine.

It’s not hard to understand why the Cowboys are making this move; Dallas has the worst defense in the NFL. They just allowed 46 points and 584 yards in a home loss to the San Francisco 49ers. The Cowboys are looking for a spark that can get them pointed in the right direction with the NFC East crown still within reach.

The Desai change famously didn’t work well for the Eagles in 2023. Their defense was even worse under Matt Patricia. But the Cowboys don’t really have any room to go but up from here.

On one hand, it’s funny to watch the Cowboys scramble like this. On the other hand, it’s unfortunate that Parker — a contributor to the Eagles’ Super Bowl LIX victory — is floundering and now being publicly embarrassed by being demoted. It would probably be more respectful for the Cowboys to fire him as opposed to keeping up this charade where he’s the defensive coordinator in title only.

item.title: Rams captain unveils how defense plays chess with quarterbacks: ‘Eyes won’t lie’
item.description: Rams captain Quentin Lake reveals how Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald force quarterbacks into mistakes ahead of a crucial Packers showdown.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams have assembled one of the best defenses in all of football. But according to team captain Quentin Lake, the team’s success this season hasn’t been the return of Myles Garrett or Aaron Donald, or the addition of All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie.

It’s the weekly chess match the Rams are winning on the field, and yes, getting some of the major pieces back on the board has allowed them to start dictating their opponent’s moves.

Sunday’s 34-6 demolition of the Arizona Cardinals offered another glimpse of what this defense can become as they continue to get healthy. The Cardinals failed to score a touchdown against the Rams in both of their meetings this season, settling for eight field goals combined.

Now, with defensive tackle Kobie Turner expected to return, the Rams could be even more dangerous when they host the Green Bay Packers on Thanksgiving Eve in a primetime showdown with enormous NFC playoff implications.

And Lake believes there’s still another gear they can reach.

“I know we’re excited to really show what it looks like to put a whole game together,” Lake told The California Post in an exclusive interview.

Lake offered a fascinating breakdown of how Garrett and Donald change the way opposing offenses operate, particularly when quarterbacks are forced to make decisions before they want to.

“Especially at safety, the eyes won’t lie,” Lake said. “Quarterbacks won’t necessarily have enough time to look you off because they’re like, ‘OK, I have to make sure this pass is going to be accurate. I have to make sure this pass is going to get there in time,’ dealing with those two guys up front.”

In other words, quarterbacks become so preoccupied with surviving the pass rush that disguising their intentions becomes an afterthought.

That gives Lake and the Rams’ secondary an opportunity to anticipate throws, jump routes and create turnovers.

But the chess match doesn’t end there.

Lake explained that opposing offensive coordinators often build their game plans around avoiding Garrett and Donald altogether, using screens, quick passes, misdirection and even waiting until one of them leaves the field before attempting a deep shot.

“Myles might not be there every single snap,” Lake said. “So he probably has something on his play sheet where it’s like, ‘Hey, these are the calls that we want when 95’s out of the game.'”

To his point, Garrett was only on the field against the Cardinals for 17 total snaps—mostly on obvious passing situations. Donald only played 23 snaps. Lake played in every defensive snap for the Rams, and as the captain, he has to recognize what their opponents are trying to do when L.A.’s biggest stars are on the sidelines catching their breath.

“So it’s a lot of chess,” Lake said.

According to Lake, the secret to winning this weekly NFL game of chess begins with stopping the run, creating negative plays on early downs and forcing quarterbacks into those obvious passing situations where the Rams can unleash Garrett and Donald together.

“We have to be able to stop the run so that you earn the right to rush the passer,” Lake said.

Once that happens, the entire defensive line, including Byron Young, Braden Fiske, and potentially Turner can pin their ears back and hunt the quarterback.

That will be crucial against the Packers, especially when the Rams’ offense is without Puka Nacua, Davante Adams and starting center Coleman Shelton. Not to mention, the availability of Steve Avila and Terrance Ferguson is still uncertain.

That puts an even greater burden on the defense to keep Los Angeles in the playoff race by beating the Packers, and Lake isn’t running from that extra responsibility.

“Anytime we can, we want to be able to carry the load,” Lake said of the Rams’ defense. “Good teams can win in any way. Whether that’s the defense carrying them, whether that’s the offense carrying them, or whether that’s being able to do special stuff in the kicking game.”

The Rams have already demonstrated they can suffocate an opponent. Against Green Bay, they’ll need to prove they can do it when the stakes are highest.

Because in a game that could help determine the NFC’s final wild-card spot, the Rams don’t just need to win the chess match, they need to make sure they put Jordan Love in checkmate.

item.title: Xavier Hutchinson, Ja'Kobi Lane highlight Week 11's Regression Files
item.description: Denny Carter takes a close look at players who might be due for positive or negative regression headed into Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
Air yards, whether we like it or not — and most fantasy folks definitely do not like it — are a good measure of a pass catcher’s opportunity and the type of passing volume in a given offense. That air yards don’t always translate into real, edible receiving yards is just part of our frustrating little game. We make small bets here and there and hope things break right from week to week and prove our process correct more often than not. It’s not any more complicated than that, even if we desperately want it to be.

Over the past few seasons I have used this space to talk mostly about guys with exceptionally high or low touchdown rates. Air yards has mostly been a side issue in the Regression Files. That will change in 2026: I want Regression Files to be your weekly go-to for (freely available) air yards data and what it means for your various fantasy football teams.

Thanks to my friend and fellow football analytics nerd Brad Beatson, we have a more organized way of not only tracking air yards data, but a measure of which pass catchers are seeing accurate targets and which guys are not. The latter phenomenon is known in nerdy football circles as Prayer Yards, or inaccurate passes that technically award a bunch of air yards to a given receiver who rarely has a chance of converting those air yards into real yards as the football sails over their head or out of bounds or wherever else.

In this space I’m going to look powerfully into total team air yards trends, players seeing plentiful prayer yards, and those who are outperforming their air yards profile and (perhaps) due for the bad kind of regression.

10 Fantasy Football Takeaways from Week 10: Emmett Johnson and Bhayshul Tuten on the rise
Emmett Johnson and Bhayshul Tuten turned in RB1 performances on the back of elite workloads in Week 10. Both running backs are poised for encores in Week 11.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

Total Team Air Yards

Below are the teams averaging the most total team air yards per game headed into Week 11.

Carolina Panthers

The fun might be over for our Panthers. They started the season as heroes for those of us who like fantasy production. They were fast-paced, they were way over their expected pass rate, and they regularly ranked among the teams putting up the most total team air yards.

That's faded of late. The Panthers over the past month rank 25th in total team air yards per game. In a Week 10 game against the Saints — a matchup I fully expected to shoot out — Carolina had a humble 246 total air yards, the 17th-most on the week. They were 5 percent below their expected pass rate, the seventh-lowest in the NFL. No Carolina pass catcher got there for fantasy purposes. It makes me question whether Jalen Coker and Darren Waller can be started in the coming weeks.

Naturally, the Panthers take on a Broncos defense this week that allows the fifth most team air yards per game.

Las Vegas Raiders

Kirk Cousins is living proof that pass attempts (and the air yards that come with them) are a quarterback stat. Cousins poured on the air yards for most of his stint as Raiders starter this season before being traded to Minnesota last week. With Cousins gone and Fernando Mendoza under center — albeit in the worst conceivable matchup — the Raiders had a measly 219 total air yards, the seventh fewest on the week. They had averaged 317 total air yards per game coming into Week 10.

The Raiders in Week 10 against Seattle were only 1.3 percent below their expected pass rate. That wouldn't be so bad if Mendoza didn't average just seven air yards per attempt. Maybe that will rise as the rookie gets more comfortable, or when he doesn't face elite defenses.

But with Brock Bowers potentially out with yet another injury and the Raiders operating at a slow offensive pace, I'm not sure if Tre Tucker, for one, is viable in this new environment.

Below are the teams averaging the fewest total team air yards per game through Week 10.

New York Jets

The Jets have trailed on 82 percent of their offensive snaps since Week 5 and their air yard totals show it. Over that miserable stretch for New York, only the Texans, Cowboys, and Packers average more total air yards per game. The Jets, in other words, are inching up on elite air yards territory.

This past week against Buffalo — a defense that regularly gives up lots of air yards — Garrett Wilson saw a whopping 193 air yards on his way to 106 yards on seven receptions. Regression Files deity Adonai Mitchell was second on the team with 119 air yards (he had three catches for 59 yards). If Omar Cooper (ankle) misses time, look for Wilson and Mitchell to split an increasingly silly number of weekly air yards in a Jets offense constantly chasing points in the second half.

The problem here is that the Jets still have the Dolphins, Chargers, and Cardinals on their schedule. Those, for now, don't look like hugely negative game script situations for the Jets. Even so, Mitchell and Wilson could be in a quietly good spot for the stretch run. Mitchell, as you might know, is running ice cold: Since Week 7, only 12 receivers have more expected fantasy points per game than the speedy deep threat. Mitchell ranks 53rd among wideouts in actual points per game over that span. So it goes.

Baltimore Ravens

Jacoby Brissett is living, breathing proof that pass attempts are a quarterback stat. There was no universe in which Brissett arrived in Baltimore and conducted a run-first, low-volume offense. And so on Monday night against the Chargers, the Ravens attempted a season-high 49 pass attempts while losing to the worst team in living memory.

I don't care about the Ravens as a team or a franchise. Probably you don't either. I only care about the volume their offense creates for fantasy-relevant players. We might have hit on something in Week 10: A Baltimore offense that is not limited to 20-25 throws per game and somewhere around 220 air yards per game. The Ravens on Monday night posted 480 total air yards, second only to the Cowboys in Week 10. That's right: The Brissett-led Ravens more than doubled the team's previous air yards average. It's a beautiful thing.

This could very well be a season-changing development for Ja'Kobi Lane and Mark Andrews (that it's a boon for Zay Flowers goes without saying). Lane saw a stunning 247 air yards against the Bolts; he came into the game averaging 29.5 air yards per outing. Probably he's never going to see another 200-air yard game, but Lane could have the makings of a high-variance flex play if this kind of pass volume keeps up for Baltimore. Incredibly, Ja'Marr Chase and George Pickens were the only wideouts in Week 10 with more expected fantasy production than Lane, who ranked WR44 in actual points.

This is objectively a better fantasy environment for Ravens pass catchers than it is when Lamar Jackson is healthy and under center.

Kansas City Chiefs

With Josh Downs running 21 percent of the team's routes — and being targeted on 61 percent of those routes — the KC offense cranked up the air yards machine in Week 10's destruction of the Falcons. Patrick Mahomes, who entered the week with a league-low 5.7 air yards per attempt, averaged 9.3 air yards per throw against Atlanta. The Chiefs' 396 team air yards — a season-high — ranked fifth in Week 10. They were 11 percent over their expected pass rate and now rank second only to the Bengals in pass rate over expected.

This would, if it holds, change the prospects of a few KC pass catchers. Rashee Rice, Cyrus Allen, and Xavier Worthy each saw about 19 percent of the team's air yards in Week 10. Downs, meanwhile, had a 17 percent air yards share on his limited route participation. Worthy was the only Kansas City receiver to run more than 63 percent of the team's routes. It's a bit of a mixed bag.

If Downs' addition to the KC offense means more downfield passing for Mahomes, that could be enough to push Downs into WR3 territory and it could make Allen a deep-league flex, however high variance. Allen does have a 44 percent air yards conversion rate, a fairly high mark for downfield guys.

▶ Prayer Yards Warrior (Players who could see positive regression)

Darius Cooper (PHI)

Prayer yards rate: 72 percent

Cooper, in Joe Milton's first game as Eagles starter, was the unofficial air yards eater in the deleted Philly offense. He had 113 air yards (a 47 percent share) in Week 9 while leading Eagles pass catchers with an 84 percent route rate. Cooper ranked top-10 in air yards that week. It's good stuff.

Milton's haywire accuracy led to a horrifyingly low 17 percent air yards conversion rate for Cooper in Week 9. My position here is that if Cooper retains his air yards eater role in Week 11 — and DeVonta Smith remains sidelined — he should see at least a little positive regression.

Xavier Hutchinson (HOU)

Prayer yards rate: 68 percent

Hutchinson is on a heater in a Houston offense that produces more total air yards per week than any team not quarterbacked by Jordan Love. He has touchdowns in three straight games, running 78 percent of the team's routes and leading the Texans in air yards over their past two games.

Yards have been harder to come by for Hutchinson. He has just three games with more than 50 receiving yards this season, and he's averaging 13.8 fantasy points per game over Houston's past two outings (while averaging 10.9 expected points per game). It's not a bad role, per se, but for now it requires touchdowns. That is, if Hutchinson's air yards conversion rate remains miserably low. That makes some sense for a wideout with an average depth of target of 12.5 yards.

Hutchinson profiles as an interesting option in an air yards-rich Houston offense that should be able to support at least a couple fantasy-viable pass catchers every week. And yes, he seems to be due for a visit from the (positive) Regression Reaper in the coming weeks.

▶ Bullseye Enjoyers (Players who could see negative regression)

George Pickens (DAL)

Bullseye rate: 50 percent

When a guy sees 299 air yards in a single game, I am required by federal law to write about him. Look it up if you don't believe me. The Supreme Court has been very clear on this. I have no choice.

By now you surely know Pickens went berserk against the Niners in Week 10 to the tune of 145 yards and three touchdowns. A week after Jerry Jones said the reason the Cowboys suck this season is because Pickens isn't seeing enough looks, Pickens had an otherworldly 35 expected fantasy points (and 43 actual points). Pickens, who had averaged a mere 87 air yards per game coming into Week 10, now ranks sixth among all receivers in air yards.

The Cowboys in Week 10 were 4 percent over their expected pass rate. It was the first time they had been over their expected pass rate since Week 6. They went run-heavy in a few games and NFL pundits called it "real football" or whatever. There's always incentive (in the form of media praise) to establish the run, even though it's usually stupid and ineffective. So maybe Dallas is done with that silly experiment and we can get back to the only reason the team exists: To fill up our fantasy box scores.

This week the Cowboys take on a Titans defense that profiles as a pass funnel and allows the eighth most total team air yards per game. Pickens should have a real chance to stay red hot here. I just needed the good Regression Files readers to know how ridiculous and unsustainable his air yards profile was in Week 10.

Ryan Flournoy (DAL)

Bullseye rate: 90 percent

The above bullseye rate — also known as air yards conversion rate — is over the past four games. In Week 10, Flournoy turned a 10 percent air yards share into six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown. His expected fantasy production over the past four games is about four points per game lower than his actual production. That's a red flag, as you probably know.

Flournoy has run extremely hot and has so far avoided a visit from the (negative) Regression Reaper. I'm not sure how much longer that can hold up unless the Dak Prescott logs 50 drop backs a week, every week.

▶ Good Air Yards Matchups: Week 11

Commanders vs. Bengals

WAS total team air yards allowed per game: 314 (6th)
CIN total team air yards allowed per game: 295 (15th)

It's not exactly bold for a football blogger to tell you a game with a 52.5-point total is a potential shootout. This one could have an absurd amount of air yards on both sides, however, putting a few secondary and tertiary guys in play.

That includes Chig Okonkwo — coming off his hideously awful Week 10 performance — and Treylon Burks, the Commanders' best downfield threat and a verified air yards eater. On the Cincy side, consider Mike Gesicki as a deep league tight end play against a Washington defense allowing the third most fantasy points per target to tight ends this season.

Titans vs. Cowboys

TEN total team air yards allowed per game: 313 (8th)
DAL total team air yards allowed per game: 301 (12th)

The Tennessee defense is going to bleed fantasy production to all comers in the coming weeks after the team traded away their only decent defensive players ahead of the NFL's trade deadline. Since Week 8, the Titans have given up the league's highest yards per play, the second-highest EPA per play, and the third-highest offensive success rate.

This is the kind of thing that forces an otherwise conservative offense to increase play volume and pass attempts as they chase points. That's exactly what we're going to get from the Titans down the stretch, including this week against the awful Dallas defense.

Since Week 7, the Titans are allowing a league-high 404 total air yards per game. That puts everyone in play on the Dallas side. Carnell Tate, if he returns from injury this week, could see a boatload of air yards, along with Elic Ayomanor, who in Week 10 ranked 16th among all receivers in air yards (87) and has accounted for 45 percent of the Titans' air yards over the past two games.

item.title: Three L.A. suspects sought in burglary of top NFL rookie Max Iheanachor's Pittsburgh home
item.description: Pittsburgh police issued three arrest warrants in connection with a burglary at the home of Steelers first-round pick Max Iheanachor.
item.content:encoded:
Arrest warrants for three Los Angeles residents were issued by Pittsburgh police Tuesday regarding a burglary at the home of Steelers’ first-round draft pick Max Iheanachor.

The U.S. Marshals Service is assisting the Pittsburgh Police Department in locating and arresting Winter Brantley, 25, Andre Castle Jr., 23, and Lamar Stewart, 45. All three face charges of burglary, criminal trespassing, theft by unlawful taking, receiving stolen property and conspiracy, according to a Pittsburgh Police Department release.

Iheanachor, an offensive tackle who attended L.A. King Drew High School and East L.A. College, had his home in the Mount Washington neighborhood of Pittsburgh burglarized Aug. 26, a day before the Steelers’ final preseason game in Buffalo. Iheanachor, 23, reported that approximately $200,000 worth of jewelry and designer bags were stolen.

Read more:ESPN analyst and former NFL coach Rex Ryan charged with running over the feet of pedestrians in Nashville

Iheanachor’s roommate, Ashley Brantley, is the brother of Winter Brantley, according to the criminal complaint. Ashley Brantley told investigators he and his sister had been quarreling. Neighborhood security cameras helped identify an Audi SUV at Iheanachor’s home the day of the burglary and credit card receipts established that the suspects rented the vehicle, police said.

On the day of the burglary, two occupants of the home had locked the doors and closed the garage, they said, before leaving for about three hours, according to police. When they returned, a window had been broken and the garage was open.

Iheanachor moved to L.A. at age 13 from Nigeria and played basketball at King Drew High. He did not play organized football until he attended East L.A. College in 2021, appearing in one game at tight end. He moved to tackle in 2022 and a year later transferred to Arizona State, where played three years before the Steelers took him with the 21st overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. The 6-foot-6, 321-pound right tackle has been the starter since the third week of the season.

item.title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: Who is Jacksonville’s Midseason MVP?

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country.

With a 7-2 record about halfway through the 2026 NFL season, the Jacksonville Jaguars are tied for third in win percentage (.778) and rank top three in FPI and DVOA efficiency metrics. They lead the league in point differential (+125).

It’s not a conversation.

Lawrence is the main catalyst of this team. Outside of the quarterback position, though, it’s a toss-up between a few guys for Midseason MVP.

Two of this year’s stars had big cleats to fill. Ventrell Miller replaced All-Pro linebacker Devin Lloyd and currently leads his position in PFF grade; Bhayshul Tuten filled in for 1,000-yard rusher Travis Etienne and is on pace to score 15 touchdowns.

DaVon Hamilton probably deserved to be an option for this survey. Walker Little deserves a shoutout for filling in more than admirably at left tackle. And Cam Little has been automatic.

item.title: 3 up and 3 down: The Midseason Edition
item.description: Drake London is hyper-reliable, but other Falcons have been anything but that.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons have played roughly 60% of their games, so this is the perfect time for a midseason 3 up and 3 down to see whose stock has risen the most and who’s taken the biggest hit.

Here’s the Week 10 edition.

3 up

Drake London

The touchdown numbers have taken a hit, but don’t get it twisted, Drake London has been worth every penny. I know he had a drop in the Chiefs game, but that’s a rare occurrence for the wideout; it was only his second this season. This man has dealt with constant quarterback shuffling, bad offensive coordinators, and no consistent running mate, but he still gets the job done.

Heading into the bye, London has the 7th-most receiving yards in the league, and his inaccurate quarterback is suppressing those numbers. He’s the best blocking receiver on the team, and you never have to worry about his effort. You’re always going to get the best version of him.

Gervon Dexter Sr.

Dexter was one of a handful of players who got an in-season extension, and he’s been living up to it. He’s second in pressures (30) on the team, the 5th most among all interior defensive linemen, and his 15.2 pass-rush win rate is 6th best for his position. He also has the second most sacks on the team.

Acquired via trade right before the season, he had a lot to prove in this new environment but has fit well in this attacking front. He still needs work in the run game; he doesn’t handle doubles well, but he still has the 3rd most run stops on the team with 10. If he can keep improving that area of his game, he’ll be one of the best overall interior players in the league.

Chris Lindstrom

There may be issues on this offensive line, but Lindstrom is not one of them. In true pass sets, he’s only allowed eight pressures and one sack across 10 games. He’s also shown that he can play in this new scheme and be a weapon as a puller. Unfortunately, he’s playing next to arguably the worst run-blocking tackle in the league, and his former center, Ryan Neuzil, wasn’t a fit, making it even harder for Lindstrom to thrive. Doesn’t matter to Lindstrom; he’s shown up every week and done his job. The team needs to get him some help this offseason so he’s not doing it alone.

Honorable Mentions: Sydney Brown, Bijan Robinson, and LaCale London

3 down

Michael Penix Jr

It’s been a mixed bag for the quarterback, and that’s not what you want to hear when you’re auditioning for your future. At this rate, I am not confident he’ll get his 5th-year option picked up. There have been flashes of good quarterback play, but not enough to give anyone confidence he’s the franchise’s future. The Falcons need the quarterback that showed up to the 49ers game, not the one they’ve had since. While accuracy has always been an issue, Penix has done a good job of protecting the ball, but we aren’t seeing that this year.

Lately, his good play doesn’t come until the game is out of hand. It also isn’t a good sign that in the 2/3 wins where he looked good, his backfield put up 200 yards on the ground. He isn’t elevating the offense, and he is cracking under pressure while facing it at the second-lowest rate (28.7%) in the league.

Penix isn’t playing for his 5th year anymore; he’s playing for his job in 2027. If the team keeps losing, they may end up with the opportunity to grab a new quarterback or feel forced to spend more money than they’d like on the market. 

Divine Deablo

A player many of us had hoped would become a piece for the future is playing himself out of Atlanta. Deablo has been bad out of the gate. His play recognition has regressed, and he looks like a shell of himself. He was dealing with a hamstring to start the season and is once again wearing a club.

The team scratched him for the Chiefs game, and hopefully the bye week does his body some good. Unfortunately, injuries are a feature of his player profile. He’s missed time every year of his career with something, and you can’t commit significant dollars to someone who can’t stay on the field. 

AJ Terrell

When cornerbacks fall off, they fall hard. This season had the makings of a special storyline with the addition of his younger brother; now the Falcons have to handle this situation carefully to prevent any bad blood. There were some lapses before Terrell went on IR, but since coming back, he’s been a disaster. It’s one thing to get torched by Ja’Marr Chase; it’s another to get worked by Cyrus Allen, giving him his first touchdown of the year. There is no easy out of this contract; the best the Falcons can hope for is that he comes off the bye, looks serviceable, and gives them enough confidence to roll into 2027 for one last ride. 

Dishonorable Mentions: Mike Hughes, Jawaan Taylor, and Olamide Zaccheaus

The Falcons have seven games left, and everyone on this list has a chance to improve or lower their stock heading into the offseason. It ain’t over till it’s over, and this evaluation period will be critical in helping the Falcons build their 2027 roster. Who will you be keeping an eye on during the final stretch?
