item.title: Eagles News: Zack Baun is a rare bright spot on this team
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 11/18/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Zack Baun is allowing just a 77.6 passer rating when targeted this season, which is slightly below his 79.2 mark from his All-Pro season in 2024. Baun is currently tied with Fred Warner as the NFL’s fifth-highest graded linebacker by Pro Football Focus. He’s a rare bright spot in this dark campaign.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

NFL Week 10: 32 teams, 32 observations – PFF

Philadelphia Eagles. Among the 84 linebackers with at least 10 targets this season, Zack Baun has the second-highest forced-incompletion rate at 18.5%. He has five forced incompletions on 27 targets.

Eagles Film Review: What to make of Makai Lemon so far – BGN

I wanted to use the bye week to get a better idea of what the Eagles have in Makai Lemon. So I went back through every target from the first nine games, hoping to see how his rookie season was developing. By the end, I was probably more frustrated with the offense than I was when I started. Evaluating a first-round receiver when almost everything thrown his way is a hitch, a quick out, or an underneath crosser is incredibly difficult. At times, this felt like an Eagles’ offense disaster compilation, with Lemon unfortunately involved. His production has improved. After 18 catches for 127 yards through six games, he caught 19 passes for 185 yards and a touchdown over the next three. However, the bigger question for me is how much more he can offer. The Eagles have given us a pretty clear picture of the role they want him to play right now. They have given us far less evidence of what he could become. All statistics in this article are courtesy of Fantasy Points Data Suite. I liked Lemon as a prospect because he looked like a good football player with a fairly high floor. I still see that. I also questioned his explosiveness and whether he could become a really good receiver. Halfway through his rookie season, too many of those questions remain unanswered because his usage has been so boring.

NFL Week 11 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we’re hearing – ESPN

Quarterback Joe Milton is poised to start his second consecutive game for the Eagles offense, which is coming off a bye week. The Eagles haven’t announced this but the signs are pointing to Milton from what I’m hearing. Whispers of a Tanner McKee return persisted after Milton took seven sacks and lost a fumble in the team’s Week 9 loss to the Giants. But Milton has owned up to missing protections, and he should be more well-versed in them due to extra preparation time off the bye. Also, Milton has the mobility to help a struggling rushing attack.

Three practice squad players around the NFL the Eagles should consider poaching – PhillyVoice

2) Michael Trigg (24), TE, Cowboys (6’4, 240). Trigg is a playmaker who had 50 catches for 694 receiving yards (13.9 YPC), and six TDs for Baylor in 2025. He finished third in the nation among tight ends in receiving yards. He’s a smaller tight end at 6’4, 240, but he has a wide catch radius because of his massive wingspan, which should also help him as a blocker. […] He also fights for every yard after the catch and is a surprisingly good route runner. I thought Trigg could go as high as Day 2 in the 2026 draft. Instead, he went undrafted because of character concerns. Longtime Cowboys beat Clarence Hill noted a couple weeks ago that Trigg is a developmental player “on and off the field.” If his off-field issues are workable, Trigg makes sense as a guy you can add to the roster, and then he’s yours all offseason to determine if he’s worth the effort in 2027 and beyond. But there’s no question that he has talent.

Roob’s bye week stats: It’s awful but we do have Makai Lemon and Dallas Goedert – NBCSP

FIRST TIME EVER: The Eagles are averaging 4.29 yards per play and allowing 5.37 yards per play. This is the first time in franchise history they’ve gained under 4.3 yards per play and allowed over 5.3 yards per play through nine games. The 4.29 is their worst on offense since 1999.

Steelers WR Roman Wilson trending towards playing vs. Eagles – Behind The Steel Curtain

The 84th pick in the 2024 NFL Draft has already posted a career high in receiving yards this season with 188 in five games played. Wilson had emerged as a downfield threat for Rodgers and one of the Steelers’ best man coverage beaters before his injury. Wilson’s return should provide a boost to the Steelers’ passing game that has been lackluster for several weeks now.

NFL Fantasy 2026 Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: Defenses for Week 11 – NFL.com

START — STEELERS DEFENSE/SPECIAL TEAMS. Over their seven-game losing streak starting in Week 3, the Eagles have allowed the third-highest pressure rate (42.8%) and fifth-most sacks per game (3.4), while scoring a league-low 14.3 points per game. Pittsburgh’s D/ST is a top-tier play once again in Week 11.

Quinyon Mitchell is consistent in his consistency – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

Cornerbacks in the NFL must be able to maintain focus to play at a high level week in and week out, a harder task than it seems. A player they are covering may only be targeted four times in a game, meaning cornerbacks spend the vast majority of their snaps matching a receiver’s routes without ever seeing a pass come their way. Yet, Quinyon Mitchell never seems to let his guard down. “He can shut down one side of the field and that makes my job easier because I know he is going to do what he’s supposed to do,” safety Andrew Mukuba said of his teammate. “It gives me that opportunity and ability to just roam around and be able to make plays.” After playing right outside cornerback all season, the first-team All-Pro shadowed a receiver for the first time this year in Week 9 against New York. His assignment? Giants Pro Bowl pass catcher Malik Nabers. Mitchell lined up against Nabers on 80 percent (24 of 30) of the star receiver’s snaps, only allowing two catches for 7 yards while in coverage despite Nabers coming off four straight 100+ receiving-yard games. What makes him such a tough matchup for receivers? “He’s very confident in himself,” wide receiver Darius Cooper said. “He’s very strong and his ball skills are increasing as well. But I think his main attributes are his confidence in himself, his strength, and he has good feet as well.”

Eagles Autism Foundation staff shine on game day – GMA

ABC News’ Will Reeve visits Lincoln Financial Field to meet neurodivergent employees helping make Philadelphia Eagles game days special through the team’s commitment to autism inclusion.

Chiefs sign former Eagles offensive lineman to practice squad – Arrowhead Pride

Fred Johnson is an eight-year veteran who started his career with the Cincinnati Bengals as an undrafted free agent out of Florida in 2019. He started eight games over three years, but the most time he has seen on the field has been the last four years with the Eagles. Johnson started in 14 regular-season games in 2024 and 2025; he also played in all four playoff games through beating Kansas City in the Super Bowl. He primarily lined up at right tackle (726 snaps) during that time, but he also played 419 snaps at left tackle.

Colts sign WR Quez Watkins to 53-man roster from practice squad, place LB Jaylon Carlies on injured reserve – Colts.com

The Indianapolis Colts today signed wide receiver Quez Watkins to the 53-man roster from the practice squad and placed linebacker Jaylon Carlies on the Injured Reserve list. Watkins, 6-0, 193 pounds, was elevated in Week 10 vs. Miami but did not play. He was originally signed to the team’s practice squad on October 6, 2026. Watkins has appeared in 49 career games (25 starts) in his time with the Colts (2026), Philadelphia Eagles (2020-23, 2025), Arizona Cardinals (2025) and Pittsburgh Steelers (2024). He has totaled 98 receptions for 1,249 yards (12.7 avg.) and six touchdowns. Watkins has also registered 14 kickoff returns for 200 yards (14.3 avg.).

Shane Steichen’s offensive game plan continues to raise serious questions despite Colts victory – Stampede Blue

Where is the offensive creativity? Steichen’s reputation as an offensive mastermind is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with what Indianapolis has actually produced on the field. Jones has looked uncomfortable in the pocket, frequently struggling when his first read isn’t available and appearing increasingly hesitant when asked to make difficult throws. His accuracy, decision-making and overall confidence have deteriorated considerably compared with his better performances in 2025 and earlier this season, yet the Colts continue operating an offense that often asks him to execute concepts he simply isn’t handling effectively right now. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Indianapolis has operated out of 11 personnel on approximately 59 percent of its offensive plays this season, meaning 1 running back, 1 tight end and 3 wide receivers. That is not an unusual formation in today’s NFL, but it becomes considerably less appealing when your receiving corps is primarily composed of backups and special teams contributors. There is nothing inherently wrong with 11 personnel, and the Colts do use different formations and motion within their existing offense. However, the question is whether those looks are actually producing meaningful advantages for the players Indianapolis currently has available. When the receivers aren’t consistently getting open and the quarterback is struggling to progress through his reads, continuing to rely on familiar concepts without making substantial adjustments becomes difficult to justify.

5 NY Giants-Jacksonville Jaguars storylines: Time to step up in class – Big Blue View

Entering the heavyweight division. When the two teams line up on Sunday, it will mark the first time this season the Giants will look across the field at a team with a winning record. The 6-4 Los Angeles Rams are currently the only winning team the Giants have faced, but the Rams were 0-1 when the teams met. Los Angeles won that game, 28-6. The Giants lost quarterback Jaxson Dart seven plays into that game, so perhaps that blowout is not indicative of how the Giants stack up. Five of the Giants’ final eight games this season are against teams with winning records. Whether they win on Sunday or not, how competitive the Giants are might tell us a lot about how well or how poorly the remainder of the season might go for the NFC East division leaders.

BREAKING: Cowboys taking play-calling duty from defensive coordinator Christian Parker – Blogging The Boys

It goes without saying that this is a rather seismic decision. Parker is in his first season with the Cowboys, obviously his first as their defensive coordinator, and it is his first season ever calling plays in general. Revoking that puts his future in doubt for the Cowboys, but that is obviously a discussion for another day. ESPN’s Todd Archer noted in his report of the news that Mike Pettine, senior defensive assistant, is set to call plays moving forward. This makes sense in the vacuum of the moment, but considering that Pettine joined the Cowboys only a month ago (after the Buccaneers loss and before the Packers game) it isn’t exactly the most organized operation at the moment.

Commanders open practice window for Jacory Croskey-Merritt to return – Hogs Haven

The Commanders have opened the 21-day practice window for running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt to return off injured reserve, the team announced on Tuesday afternoon. Washington’s practice week formally starts on Thursday, which will be the first time he’ll hit the practice field after being placed on IR with a groin injury. Croskey-Merritt had been battling the injury since training camp, and Washington chose to shelf him rather than trying to manage the injury from week to week, allowing him to heal properly.

Raiders-Browns flexed to ‘Sunday Night Football,’ for some reason – SB Nation

We won’t be waiting all week for Sunday night when it comes to Week 12 in the NFL. The league announced on Tuesday afternoon that they’re were shaking up the schedule with the flex, thankfully getting Patriots vs. Chargers the hell off primetime TV — but they’re replacing it with …. Raiders vs. Browns. This will certainly be fun, at least in some ways. Cleveland is always an incredible home stadium and Browns fans will be raucous; it’ll be neat to see Fernando Mendoza in his first primetime game since taking over as the Raiders starting quarterback. That is the end of the excitement for this game.

item.title: Examining Bills run-heaviness in first half of 2026 campaign
item.description: Taking a deep dive into Buffalo’s run-heavy attack
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills have loved running the football thus far in the 2026 season.

James Cook has the second-most carries in the NFL right now at 187. As a team, the Bills are the current owners of the second-highest first-down designed run rate in the NFL at 61.3%.

Now, sure, the Bills have recently played in a collection of games that featured plenty of garbage time, when Buffalo has attempted to burn clock by tapping into the run game.

Even when garbage-time is considered, the Bills have the NFL’s second-highest run rate on all downs at 45.7%. The rest of the league averages a designed run play on 39.3%. Quarterback scrambles — that occur on dropbacks — and spikes and kneels are excluded in that calculation.

Analytics have proven that passing the football is more efficient than running the football. And this article isn’t going to show that the Bills have actually become more efficient on the ground than through the air.

Right now, in non-garbage time situations, Buffalo’s designed-run game has provided the team +0.023 EPA per play, the eighth-highest figure in the NFL. The team’s pass game has provided the team +0.239 EPA per dropback, the fourth-best in football. Unsurprisingly, the difference in value added for each method of moving the football has been seismic.

Up until now, the Bills have genuinely attempted to “establish” the run in their first nine games of the 2026 campaign.

Accepting that fact raises two questions: what type of play call have the Bills chosen on second down and how effective have their second downs been?

Before I begin with the results, despite an overall negative EPA in first-down run scenarios (-0.059, the 15th-highest in football), the Bills have had 16.4% of those runs gain 10+ yards. That’s the fourth-best in the NFL and much higher than the league average of 10.3%.

This is where things get fascinating for Buffalo’s elite offense. And where it has leaned on its pass game.

On second down after a first-down run — in non-garbage time scenarios, of course — the Bills have dropped back to pass 73.8% of the time, which is the fourth-highest rate in the NFL and noticeably higher than the league average of 64.5%.

On all second downs, regardless of whether a run or pass was called on first down, the Bills’ dropback rate is 66.9%, the ninth-highest in the NFL.

While the Bills are actually below league average in conventional passing statistics within both second-down parameters, they are 12th in EPA per dropback in second downs after a first down run and on all non-garbage time second downs.

An enormous element of said impressive EPA per dropback on second down for the Bills despite below-average passing statistics in those situations is of course Josh Allen scrambles, the ultimately luxury built into Buffalo’s dropback game. The possibility of an Allen scramble occurring on a dropback must be considered.

Allen has eight scrambles on second-down runs that have totaled 87 yards. That’s 10.9 yards per scramble, the second-highest average among all quarterbacks in those scenarios. His +1.162 EPA on those plays, is far and away, tops in the NFL.

You have survived this massive number dump, and I appreciate you making it this far.

Essentially, yes — the Bills have been very run heavy. But they’ve smartly morphed into being one of the league’s more pass-happy clubs on second down, and Allen’s running on second-down dropbacks have been incredibly effective.

item.title: Cowboys shake up coaching staff with weird change after defensive abomination
item.description: The Cowboys’ saga on defense continues.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys’ saga on defense continues.

After days of speculation, ESPN reported Wednesday that defensive coordinator Christian Parker will remain in his position, but senior defensive coordinator Mike Pettine will instead call defensive plays during games.

The update comes after head coach Brian Schottenheimer hesitated to give Parker a vote of confidence and ripped his defense following a 46-40 home loss to the 49ers on Sunday.

“At the end of the day, the tackling and some of the covered stuff really led to the [explosive plays],” Schottenheimer said. “I’m taking a deep dive and looking at everything.”

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones added to the speculation when he said during a radio appearance Tuesday that Parker’s position has come up in conversations, but did not give further detail.

“We’re talking about that, but I’m not going to talk about it here,” Jones said on 105.3 The Fan. “But we are talking about those things.”

The Cowboys allowed 584 total yards Sunday, the most they’ve allowed in a home game in franchise history.

They’re now ranked as the worst defense in the NFL, allowing 393.8 yards per game and 33 total touchdowns, a mark that only trails the Raiders and Cardinals.

Parker, 34, is the youngest defensive coordinator in team history and is in his first coordinator role of his career.

He spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons as Philadelphia’s defensive passing game coordinator and saw success working with Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, as well as Patrick Surtain II from his time in Denver.

Pettine served as the Browns’ head coach from 2014-15, and was previously the defensive coordinator for the Jets, Bills and Packers.

item.title: Vikings WR Jauan Jennings prepare to face his former team
item.description: Sunday night's game in Mexico City between the Vikings and 49ers has multiple interesting subplots.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday night's game in Mexico City between the Vikings and 49ers has multiple interesting subplots. One relates to a player who had spent his entire career with the 49ers before signing with Minnesota.

Jauan Jennings is in his first season as a Viking. In six games with two starts, he has only six catches for 54 yards.

And there was a strong possibility of a trade back to the 49ers. He ultimately decided to stay where he was.

The Vikings will need him on Sunday night, especially with receiver Jordan Addison out due to a thumb injury.

“With us being down Jordan Addison, we’re gonna need him to make some plays in the pass game," coach Kevin O'Connell said Tuesday on KFAN.

Jennings didn't play in Week 10 at Green Bay due to a calf injury.

During five seasons with the 49ers, Jennings caught 210 passes for 2,581 yards and 22 touchdowns in 75 regular-season games. He also had 23 catches for 289 yards and a touchdown in 11 postseason games — including four catches for 42 yards and a touchdownand a touchdown pass in Super Bowl LIX.

Without Addison, Jennings could get more opportunities. And he will surely have a little extra incentive to show his former team that they should have kept him around.

item.title: Steelers get best possible news about Mason McCormick injury
item.description: Steelers may get Mason McCormick back this season.
item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Steelers guard Mason McCormick suffered an ankle injury in the team’s Sunday night loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, leading to him having to be carted off the field in an air cast. Many assumed that McCormick’s season was over, but that may not be the case.

Per Alan Saunders, McCormick didn’t break his ankle, only dislocated it.

“Steelers LG Mason McCormick did not suffer a fracture, somehow only dislocating his right ankle, and will not require surgery, source confirms,” Saunders reports. “NFL Network first reported. He could potentially return in the playoffs.”

The Steelers will rely on Spencer Anderson to fill the left guard spot for the time being, although head coach Mike McCarthy did say rookie Gennings Dunker could become an option. Pittsburgh will face the Eagles in Philadelphia this week, a place they haven’t won in over 60 years.

item.description: How did 2025 draft class fare?
item.content:encoded:
Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2025 draft class fared in a home 21-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at the Denver Broncos.

Ashton Jeanty:

The No. 6 overall draft pick played 71 percent of the snaps, his most since Week 7. Still, his production was clacking. He has had nine carries for 18 yards. He has averaged 2.9 or less yards per carry for the sixth time this season. He did have four catches on four targets for 46 yards.

Jack Bech:

The second-round pick played 56 percent of the snaps after playing 34 percent in Week 9. Bech has not produced since returning in Week 8 from a broken forearm. He has three catches for 19 yards on nine targets in those three games. He’s just not making an impact.

Darien Porter:

The third-round pick was replaced by Zeke Masses as the starter, but he did play 53 percent of the snaps. So, he’s still in the mix.

Caleb Rogers:

The benched starter played just three special teams snaps.

Charles Grant:

The offensive lineman, taken in the third round, played three special teams snaps.

Dont’e Thornton:

The wide receiver, taken in the fourth round, has been on the 53-man roster for three games and he was inactive for all three games.

Tonka Hemingway:

The fourth-round pick played 61 percent of the snaps, the most of any Raiders’ defensive tackle.

JJ Pegues:

The defensive tackle, taken in the sixth round, was active for the fifth time this season. He played 12 defensive snaps, which is his range.

Cody Lindenberg:

The seventh-round pick played 22 snaps on special teams, which is his norm. He has played just three defensive snaps this season.

item.title: 10 Fantasy Football Takeaways from Week 10: Emmett Johnson and Bhayshul Tuten on the rise
item.description: Emmett Johnson and Bhayshul Tuten turned in RB1 performances on the back of elite workloads in Week 10. Both running backs are poised for encores in Week 11.
item.content:encoded:
Week 10 was highlighted by big-name quarterbacks doing big-name quarterback things and a pair of running backs on the rise. Headed into Week 11, these are the 10 fantasy football storylines you need to know.

NFL Week 11 Injury Report: Drake Maye likely done for season, surgery for Jordan Addison
Track the injuries to know around the NFL, all in one place.
  • Mark Garcia,
  • Nic Bodiford,

1) The GOAT is back

In Josh Downs’ first game as a Chief, Patrick Mahomes logged his first five-touchdown game since 2022. One of those went to Downs, despite the newly minted Chief running just eight routes. Mahomes notably posted his second-highest aDOT of the year at 10.1. He attempted six deep passes from the moment Tyquan Thornton went down in Week 4 until last week. He did not complete a single one of them. He threw seven deep passes on Sunday and completed four of them for 150 yards and three scores. Can we give Downs credit for this shift? Probably not entirely. Six of Mahomes’ deep passes and three of his completions were with Downs on the sidelines. At best, we can say the acquisition of Downs signaled a philosophical shift that led to more deep attempts in Week 10. I would bet on last week being Mahomes’ best game of the season. I would also bet on him being better than he was in the post-Thornton era this year, which was truly abysmal.

2) Joe Burrow on a historic pace

After another monster performance, Burrow is on pace for 5,279 yards and 48 touchdowns. With 409 yards and four touchdowns on Sunday night, Burrow has three games with 400-plus yards and four games with 4-plus touchdowns. Only three players have hit 400 yards four times in a season. The record for 4+ passing touchdown games is nine. It’s going to be hard for the Bengals to sustain this torrid pace, but their combination of volume and efficiency makes it possible. They are the 10th-best team of the past decade in EPA per dropback, but they’re also the current league-leaders in pass rate over expected. At over nine percent, it’s not a close race.

They are the fifth-best team of the past decade in total passing EPA per game. Three of the teams ahead of them are from 2020. Burrow is now the clear MVP front-runner as we head into the back half of the season.

3) Emmett Johnson goes nuclear

The rookie made his first career start last week and didn’t disappoint. He ran 22 times for 101 yards while adding six catches for 70 yards and two scores. He recorded 22.6 expected fantasy points and 35.1 actual PPR points, which was the third-best mark of the week. It looks like Kenneth Walker could miss another game, putting Johnson right back at the top of the RB1 mix. Johnson ranks third in the NFL in yards after contact per attempt (4.04) and is the runaway leader in yards per route run (3.1). He is the next generation’s Tony Pollard.

4) More backup quarterbacks take over

There’s somehow a never-ending flow of backup quarterbacks entering the mix. Carson Beck and Kyle McCord made their starting NFL debuts while Tommy DeVito played most of the game after Drake Maye left early in the first quarter. Cade Klubnik even got some run with Geno Smith going down on Sunday. Here’s how things went for the four quarterbacks.

EPA per playCPOEPFF Passing GradeAccurate Throw Rate
Carson Beck-0.61-9.474.50.529
Kyle McCord-0.12-10.947.80.448
Tommy DeVito-0.25-1839.70.524
Cade Klubnik-0.04-1.930.90.353

By just EPA, they were all bad, but Beck was atrocious. On the other hand, PFF’s charting thought he had a genuinely good performance. I don’t know if I would go that far, but Beck was hung out to dry by his receivers.

I'll admit that I was not a Carson Beck guy going in. And I expected this tape to be bad, losing 34-6 while going 11 for 18 with 2 picks.

But all three of these throws should have been caught (and one was picked). Beck could have had a totally different day. pic.twitter.com/HpDN006wtM

— Andrew Cooper (@CoopAFiasco) November 16, 2026

My main takeaway from this is that we shouldn’t panic about Trey McBride just yet.

There might be a modicum of hope for Klubnik as well. He had a dreadful passing grade, but everything else was okay. He also had the highest aDOT in the league last week at 12.0. He tried to push the ball downfield and it didn’t always work. But if you’re going to be bad, be bad and aggressive. That’s exactly what he did.

Without much in the way of redeeming stats or film for McCord and DeVito, I will be avoiding all Pats and Dolphins players for the foreseeable future.

5) Tuten’s role expands

In a relatively easy win over the Titans, the Jags did what they always do and took the air out of the football in the second half. What they didn’t do was take Tuten off the field to pile carries on the backups. He saw 76 percent of the team’s designed attempts, good for a career-high 25 carries. Tuten also ran more routes than usual, logging a 47 percent route rate plus a 12 percent target share. His 29.9 expected fantasy points were a season-high. Only Chuba Hubbard had more expected points in Week 10. Tuten’s role has been hit-or-miss every week, but he’s often smoothed over the cracks with touchdowns. If he can maintain this role and keep his efficiency high, he’ll close out the season as an RB1.

NFL Week 11 Injury Report: Drake Maye likely done for season, surgery for Jordan Addison
Track the injuries to know around the NFL, all in one place.
  • Mark Garcia,
  • Nic Bodiford,

6) Jalen Coker’s slump continues

Coker’s red hot start to the season had him poised for high-end WR2 numbers this year. He’s since fallen off the map entirely. Over the past month, Coker has seen 14 percent of Bryce Young’s targets and the downturn in opportunities could not have come at a worse time. In his past four appearances, Bryce Young has thrown for 212 yards per game. That’s down from 310 yards over his first five games. Because Coker isn’t earning targets and the offense is struggling, he’s averaging 4.6 PPR points per game over his past four outings. The Panthers get a date with a middling Baltimore defense next week. Then they face the league’s No. 1 and No. 2 defenses by EPA per dropback in the Bucs and the Vikings. If Coker doesn’t get home this week, it might be a while before he posts his next usable fantasy score.

7) Saints stars disappear

Travis Etienne got off to a bizarre start to the season, operating in a committee role despite signing a four-year, $52 million contract in the spring. He was averaging 10 carries per game over three weeks before going on injured reserve. The Saints activated him from IR ahead of Week 10, but his role was unchanged. He saw under half the designed carries for the fourth time and ran a measly 28 percent of the routes. Audric Estime saw one fewer carry than him and Alvin Kamara, who scored twice, saw one fewer target. Kamara and Estime both saw a goal line carry. Etienne did not see a look inside the five. He’s a lowly RB3 right now.

At receiver, Chris Olave’s role evaporated. He earned a 13 percent target share and 14 percent of the team’s air yards. Not only were those his lowest marks of the season, but they would have also been his lowest marks of 2025. This coincided with Jordyn Tyson’s role going to the moon. He went from a 35 percent route rate in Week 9 to a 72 percent route rate last week. His target share ballooned to 42 percent and he accounted for 53 percent of Tyler Shough’s air yards, albeit at an underwhelming 6.3 aDOT. It’s one game. We shouldn't assume Tyson has overtaken Olave in the pecking order for targets. But it’s at least on the table.

8) Chargers make some progress

Finally bringing home their first win of the season, the Chargers’ offense showed some signs of life on Monday. Omarion Hampton logged 105 rushing yards on 22 attempts, both of which are the best marks for a Chargers running back this year. Tre’ Harris hit 86 yards through the air, tying Ladd McConkey’s high-water mark from Week 1. With McConkey out, Herbert funneled targets to Harris, who earned a 33 percent target share and a massive 76 percent of the air yards. Harris also ran every single route. Quentin Johnston was on the field for most routes but earned just one target. Mike McDaniel seems to have finally given up on his dream of making Johnston a thing.

The same is true of Keaton Mitchell, who tied his season-lows in snap share (24 percent) and carry share (11 percent). On his best workload of the season, Hampton posted 3.95 yards after contact and logged two runs of 15+ yards. Those go down as season-highs for the second-year back. I doubt the Chargers are a fixed offense all of a sudden, but simplifying things and building the plane out of two players might be for the best going forward.

9) Rams personnel usage gets even weirder

Without his WR1, WR2, WR3, and TE1, who was more like the de facto WR3, Sean McVay did what he always does and got creative. McVay ditched the heavy packages with more tight ends than receivers and leaned on his running backs, even on passing plays. The Rams dropped back in 20-personnel—two running backs and zero tight ends—18 times. Stafford threw for 202 yards at 12.6 yards per attempt out of 20-personnel. Over the past four seasons, no team had attempted more than five passes out of 20. Since 2020, the record for passing yards out of 20 was 107. Even more notable is that McVay did this without a fullback on the roster. Every other notable 20-personnel game of the past seven years involved plenty of fullback snaps.

Blake Corum and Kyren Williams combined for a 34 percent target share. Corum’s mark of 15 percent was nearly double that of his previous season-high while Williams posted his second-best target share of the year. The Rams are on bye this week and could get Davante Adams back after the break, so maybe this all means nothing going forward. Still, it was fascinating to watch the best mind in football solve this problem. If Adams isn’t ready for Week 12, we’re firing up both LA backs once again.

10) Air yards sommelier Ja’Kobi Lane

Baltimore's rookie wideout didn't do much of note for fantasy managers in Week 10 with a 3/61/0 receiving line. For spreadsheet grinders like myself, his Week 10 performance was a truly special one. Lane was targeted nine times at an aDOT of 18.8, giving him 169 air yards on the week. Only three wideouts saw more air yards. Lane was also the recipient of one of Jacoby Brissett's two passes into the end zone. Brissett has the 11th-most deep passes this year, albeit with just the 27th-most completions. He hasn't been successful as a downfield passer, but that hasn't stopped him from trying. He was already better at it in his Baltimore debut, completing 50 percent of his deep shots compared to 18 percent in Arizona.

item.title: The New York Jets Need To Reimagine Their Running Back Usage
item.description: This Running Back Split Isn’t Making Much Sense To Me
item.content:encoded:
I’ll start this article with a shameless pat on the back. Despite me getting numerous things wrong throughout the years (likely more wrong than right), one thing I’ve been very happy to see develop is the breakout of Braelon Allen.

Now, for those who know my opinion on the matter, you know I’ve been pretty vocal about Allen’s potential and what he could end up being. It was rooted in a pretty simple theory: Allen is too strong, big, and fast to fail. If I had to get into a bit more detail, I could talk about how Allen possesses great contact balance, is light on his feet, showcases strong vision, and does all of this while being extremely young (he was 17 as a true freshman and just 20 when he entered the league).

One of the few positive developments for the Jets this year was just how effective Allen was when Breece Hall was injured. Look at some of these snaps just the week prior to Breece’s return:

Come on, this is some good stuff.

However, like most things with the Jets, it got complicated once Breece Hall returned. What would be a great problem to have for certain teams, two good players at the same position who complement each other well, has already become a big-time headache for the Jets. How does the staff utilize the skill sets of Breece Hall and Braelon Allen effectively? How can they both contribute as difference-makers to this team while still getting enough opportunities?

Now, it’s a small sample since Breece Hall has come back (only two games), but I’m going to make my case as to why the early usage split doesn’t make much sense to me.

Usage

From a distance, I think everyone is probably in agreement that, simply put, Braelon Allen has flashed more as a runner this year. Before we even get to the stats, I think I could get most people to agree with that just from watching the two play.

Allen fits your typical profile of a heavy-usage back. He’s big, has good vision, can break tackles, and rarely gets tackled for a loss. Breece is a bit different. Down by down, he’ll leave you with some inconsistencies. He’s heavily reliant on his breakaway speed, but that also makes him incredibly effective in the open field. He’s got a history of turning small gains into explosive ones.

A stat I remember from this offseason really reminds me of this. Since 2020, there’s only been one player with 3+ 50-yard runs and 3+ 50-yard receptions in that time frame: Breece Hall.

But now, let’s take a look at some of the rushing stats from this year. We’ll use a few metrics from Next Gen Stats that help demonstrate how Allen has been significantly more impactful as a down-to-down runner.

Here are some of the metrics we’ll be looking at:

  • Efficiency (EFF): Rushing efficiency is calculated by taking the total distance a player traveled on rushing plays as a ball carrier, according to Next Gen Stats, and dividing it by the rushing yards gained. The lower the number, the more of a north-south runner the player is.
  • 8+ Defenders in the Box (8+D%): On every play, Next Gen Stats calculates how many defenders are stacked in the box at the snap. Using that logic, this metric calculates how often a rusher sees eight or more defenders in the box against them.
  • Average Time Behind the Line of Scrimmage (TLOS): Next Gen Stats measures the amount of time a ball carrier spends behind the line of scrimmage before crossing it, measured to the nearest tenth of a second. TLOS represents the average time behind the LOS on all rushing plays where the player is the rusher.
  • Rushing Yards Over Expected (RYOE): The difference between actual yards gained and expected yards gained (Actual – Expected). This uses player tracking data, including the position, speed, and direction of the runner, blockers, and defenders at the moment of handoff, to calculate how many yards an average running back would gain in that exact scenario. A positive number means the runner created yardage beyond what the blocking and defensive alignment provided.
  • Rushing Over Expected Percentage (ROE%): Also tracked as Carries Beating Expected (%), this measures the share of a runner’s carries that gain more yardage than the NFL Next Gen Stats Expected Rushing Yards model predicts. While total RYOE can be skewed by a single massive breakout run, ROE% highlights down-to-down consistency.

Now, let’s compare:

Breece Hall:

  • 77 carries, 265 yards, 3.4 AVG
  • 4.8 EFF
  • 2.79 TLOS
  • -31 RYOE
  • 32% ROE

Braelon Allen:

  • 128 carries, 638 yards, 5.0 AVG
  • 3.41 EFF
  • 2.72 TLOS
  • 118 RYOE
  • 52% ROE

So, what do these stats tell us?

A few things. For starters, they show that Breece has been significantly less of a north-south runner than Braelon Allen has. Hall actually has the 5th highest EFF in the league, showing that he’s traveling a lot of distance on plays without getting much to show for it. That also shows up in his RYOE and ROE numbers. He ranks in the bottom 10 in ROE%, something Hall has historically struggled with due to his home-run running style. He’s actually performed worse than what would be expected from an average back and that’s shown with the -31 RYOE.

To Breece’s credit, he’s normally better than this. He may have been hampered by the injury earlier this year. Again, he has a tendency to make up for some of these inconsistencies with a handful of explosive runs. But the numbers this year have been pretty telling.

Allen, though, has been quite frankly terrific. He’s top 8 in RYOE and yards per carry this year. He hasn’t showcased the historic explosiveness that Hall has, but Allen actually ranks #1 in the league in ROE%. That shows that Allen is rarely leaving yards on the field. He doesn’t have the home-run ability Hall has, and probably never will, but if you need a workhorse back who consistently churns out positive yards, keeps the offense above the sticks, and prevents the team from getting into bad situations, there legitimately hasn’t been a better back in the NFL at that this year than Allen.

But the running back position isn’t just about running. We also have to consider how each back performs on passing downs.

From a pass-protection perspective, there’s not a ton to glean from the numbers. Hall has historically graded decently in most metrics. He’s never been great, but he’s usually around average by PFF grade and ranks 19th out of 60 backs this year. He’s not a liability.

Allen, quietly, has been great in this regard according to PFF. In an extremely small sample last year, his grade would have been good enough to finish as a top-2 back. This year, he ranks 6th in PFF grade. Based on what we’ve seen over the last season and a half, it’s probably fair to say Allen is a well above-average pass protector.

Now, what about receiving?

This is where Hall has the clear advantage, both in the stats and on film. Let’s take a look:

Breece Hall:

  • 17 catches, 18 targets, 195 yards
  • 2.71 Yards Per Route Run
  • 6 Missed Tackles Forced
  • 8 First Downs

Braelon Allen:

  • 20 catches, 24 targets, 108 yards
  • 0.68 Yards Per Route Run
  • 6 Missed Tackles Forced
  • 6 First Downs

What does this data show?

Hall is far, far better as a pass-catcher. And while the yards per route run number will likely normalize (it’s better than 95% of NFL wide receivers right now), Hall has consistently been a more than effective pass-catcher throughout his career.

His career yards per route run is 1.59, a very good pace for a running back. For context, Jahmyr Gibbs sits at 1.56 yards per route run in his career. Christian McCaffrey and Alvin Kamara, probably the two best backs in recent memory at catching passes out of the backfield, have career yards per route run numbers of 1.73 and 1.80, respectively.

Hall isn’t quite at that level, but the numbers show he really is not too far off.

It makes sense, too, when you see the way he moves and runs routes and moves with the ball in space:

The burst, straight-line speed, and open-field ability are all on display. Using him as a pass-catcher allows Hall to showcase his strongest attributes.

So, what have we settled on after looking at all this data?

To me, it paints a pretty clear picture this year. Braelon Allen has limitations as a pass-catcher, but he’s a terrific runner. If you need someone to consistently churn out positive yards and keep the offense in good situations, he’s your guy. Breece Hall can struggle mightily at times as a rusher, but he’s super effective in the open field and is one of the best pass-catchers at his position and is good for a handful of explosive runs a season.

On paper, this seems like a pretty easy fix. Give Allen the majority of the rushing carries, while spelling him at times with Breece to try to hit the explosive runs. Give Breece the majority of the passing downs, until you plan on using Allen at times to protect the QB as an extra blocker.

But here’s the problem: The Jets have not done this.

The Usage

And this is where my problem lies. I’m not sure I have much trust in the Jets staff to leverage both of these guys to their optimal potential. Because, to this point, the data will show that the Jets are almost doing the exact opposite of what you’d expect them to do.

Now, disclaimer: This is a small sample. Perhaps there’s a reason for this through two weeks that I haven’t seen. (Although I don’t want to give the Jets the benefit of the doubt when they’ve been adamant in press conferences that Breece is their “workhorse.”)

Simply looking at the last two weeks, here’s how the Jets have used both backs.

Total Snaps:

  • Breece Hall: 68
  • Braelon Allen: 70

Rushing Snaps:

  • Breece Hall: 28
  • Braelon Allen: 18

Pass-Protection Snaps:

  • Breece Hall: 10
  • Braelon Allen: 15

Pass-Route Snaps:

  • Breece Hall: 29
  • Braelon Allen: 35

Now, there are a couple of snaps where both were lined up, which might skew the overall numbers, but this data shows a pretty clear picture. Allen has actually run more routes over the last two weeks and has been on the field for more of the passing work (roughly 56% of it), while Hall has gotten more of the action in the run game (getting nearly 61% of the work).

To me? Based on the data we’ve looked at, this is almost the exact opposite of what should be happening.

It’s pretty clear to me that Hall should be getting the majority of the passing-game action, while Allen gets the majority of the run-game action. I understand Allen getting some action in the passing game (he’s a better pass-blocker than Breece), but there’s really no reason he should be running more routes than Hall over a two-game stretch.

And listen, I get the argument the Jets coaches would try to make. I understand that game script can have an impact on a two-game sample. Being at the game Sunday, I have to believe that during the two-minute drill at the end of the first half, Allen got that work in large part because Breece was out the drive before. They probably wanted to go with the fresher guy who had just gotten a series off.

However, I’m just not sure this is a good enough excuse, and as of right now, I don’t have enough trust that the Jets staff will actually maximize these two players.

If you’re expecting to get the ball at the end of a half in a pass-heavy situation, then even if Breece was out the series before, he likely should still be the one getting those snaps. And simply put, a staff should be planning for this. That exact scenario is easily avoidable by giving Allen more work earlier in the game, allowing Breece to be fresher by the time the game script changes and the Jets find themselves in more pass-heavy situations.

Conclusion:

Earlier in this series, I was a pretty big “trade Breece” guy. But the more I look into each of these guys from a data and stats perspective, the more I think there’s legitimate reason to keep both around.

On paper, these guys complement each other perfectly. Allen’s strengths are Breece’s weaknesses. Breece’s strengths are Allen’s weaknesses.

Like I said, I normally think Jets coaching staffs tend to get too much hate at times, particularly because the talent tends to be lacking around these parts. However, in this particular case, I really do think this staff is not utilizing both of these guys to their optimal potential.

We’ll see if anything changes down the stretch. I wouldn’t count on it. But going forward, long-term, I think this is a pretty easy fix. You have two talented running backs with completely different skill sets, and there’s a legitimate way to get both guys on the field a strong amount.

You just need a competent staff to figure it out.

item.title: Where does the Cowboys defense go from here?
item.description: The Cowboys defense is a unit in crisis
item.content:encoded:
Coming into this season, the world had moderately low expectations for a Dallas Cowboys defense in the middle of a rebuild, paired with a first-time defensive coordinator. Given the offseason moves and what we saw in Oxnard, there was no reason things shouldn’t have at least been a little bit better than last season. If nothing else, it couldn’t possibly be worse for a defense that would have ranked 40th in 2025 if there were 40 NFL teams. Then 2026 hit us like a ton of bricks.

The numbers

The first-year Christian Parker defense ranks last in nearly every metric across the league. Dallas ranks last or near last in total yards allowed per game, rush yards per game, third-down conversion rate allowed, while also failing to contain explosive plays week after week.

Despite possessing a top five scoring offense in the NFL, the Cowboys are just 4-6. While the offense isn’t without flaws of their own, the clearest reason for most losses comes down to a historically bad defensive performance.

The Cowboys are once again on track to set all the wrong defensive records just one season after setting all the wrong defensive records.

What’s going wrong

This failure isn’t just a one year collapse. It’s the continuation of a multi-year slide that began after their peak during the Dan Quinn years where Dallas had a top five ranked defense in 2022 and 2023. Dallas has gone through defensive coordinators each year after the Quinn departure with Mike Zimmer, Matt Eberflus, and now Christian Parker. The front office spent the last year and a half spending draft capital, making big trades, and signing free agents to fix that side of the ball, yet the returns on investment are yet to be discovered.

Parker, 34 and in his first defensive coordinator job is struggling to install a functional unit that won’t break down in tackling, communication, and scheme execution. While the pass rush has gotten significantly better since adding Mike Pettine to the staff, who is now taking over as the defensive play caller, the defense as a whole still suffers from an inability to execute the most basic functions of sound defense.

The defensive line, including the edge group, plays undisciplined football. Setting the edge and staying disciplined seems to be something that the ends just simply aren’t interested in, as displayed by the Deebo Samuel reverse play against the 49ers. Quinnen Williams is the lone, consistent bright spot up front for the Cowboys.

The secondary has been uneven with rookie Caleb Downs and Joey Porter Jr. playing the best amongst the group. Downs has hit some rookie bumps, as to be expected, but he’ll clearly be a good player in the NFL. Porter Jr. is a difference maker, consistently shutting down the short side of the field. But the gap between those two players and the rest of the secondary is too great to overcome.

The floor of the players on the Cowboys defense appears to be too low and the first-year defensive coordinator has not done enough to raise it. They’ll play multiple quarters of, at worst, acceptable football. And then out of nowhere, the dam breaks thanks to a simple screen, blown coverage, or big run play. Dallas has simply been unable to put an end to this cycle week after week and it’s costing them games.

Where it goes from here

In the short term, there is no easy fix. The foundations have been laid and Dallas now turns the defensive play-calling duties to Mike Pettine in hopes of better gameday results. Dallas was heavily focused on improving the football intelligence and ability of the players on the defense, but are now looking to simplify the calls according to Brian Schottenheimer.

With that in mind, there is still a more than small chance for the Cowboys to make the playoffs in 2026. The Giants schedule is hitting their tough stretch, while the Cowboys have a couple of easy games ahead. That may not mean much, however, as we’ve seen the Cowboys lose to bad teams like the Buccaneers and Cardinals, so they can lose to anybody. If the defense can clean up the most fundamental issues such as tackling and lane discipline, this team may stand a chance at winning the NFC East. If not, we’ll continue to witness struggles against even the worst teams in the league.

For 2027 and beyond, the Cowboys find themselves in a tough situation to navigate. Salary cap restructures or cuts with DaRon Bland, Kenny Clark, Rashan Gary and others are looming. The biggest decision of the offseason may come down to Joey Porter Jr. versus George Pickens and who gets a new deal. Losing either player significantly hurts the ability on their respective side of the ball. Dallas will also have to make decisions on their coaching staff from the head coach down. The entire picture is muddy as the defensive rebuild continues, maybe even requiring another step back to properly build it out moving forward.

Dallas spent significant resources in the middle of 2025 and in 2026 trying to remake the defense into a respectable unit this season. Unfortunately, the results have not matched the investment. With time running out of the season, the next several weeks will determine what happens with this coaching staff and how much rope the front office will allow them to course correct this year and beyond.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Trade-deadline acquisitions immediately make their presence felt
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen goes over the first performances of some of the noteworthy trade pickups made in Week 10.
item.content:encoded:
Like most fans, I'm a prisoner of the moment. I may or may not have made declarative statements about the Bengals, their QB's claim to an MVP and the team's chances of winning a Super Bowl after they beat the brakes off the Steelers. But, to quote Joe Burrow: "No one winning the division with seven wins." Or, said another way, we should let things marinate before making judgments.

The ramp-up to the NFL Trade Deadline gave us a few skill players switching teams. All were instant contributors. So, with an extra couple of days to sit with their performances, let's check in on each and their fantasy outlook for the rest of the season. 

All right, Minnesota. You have my Attention.

Eight completions. That was Carson Wentz's answer to whether the Vikings should acquire a new QB. DC Brian Flores' defense handed Josh Allen his second-lowest EPA per dropback in the first half of any game this season. Wentz responded with the sixth-fewest completions of any passer to have 25 or more dropbacks in a single game since the start of the decade. Minnesota's front office had to do something. And the early returns have them right back in the race to take home the Lombardi Trophy. 

After 3 years away, Kirk Cousins returns to the Vikings following a trade deadline reunion.

21/31, 207 PASS YDS, 2 TD, 1 INT vs Packers.

Minnesota's Super Bowl odds improved immediately after the trade. Can Cousins take them all the way? https://t.co/kp439AqYUApic.twitter.com/YvyjTA8oky

— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 15, 2026

If you look at the box score, not much stands out about Kirk Cousins' first day back in purple. Just crept over the 200-yard mark in passing yards. He joined his predecessors in taking three or more sacks. Even floated a meatball sub out to the defense. Of course, Cousins only had two full practices with the team before Sunday's game. Besides, the real changes happened under the hood of the offense. 

  • Early-Down PROE: -4.5% (Wentz), -1.8% (Murray), +4.7% (Cousins)

  • Play-Action Rate: 33.3%, 44.0%, 50.0%

  • Avg. Time to Throw: 2.68, 2.98, 2.47

Let's start with the basic idea that if the offense just ran more plays and soaked up more clock, they could take pressure off of the defense. With Wentz, the offense leaned on the run game, ran 48.5 plays per game and had an average 22:23 time of possession. Murray brought more passing, leading to more snaps (60.2 a week), bringing their time of possession up to 32:03. Minnesota was up to 65 plays and held the ball for over 35 minutes against the Packers.

On just two days of practice, HC Kevin O'Connell opted for his QB to throw more on early downs. The result was two-fold. First, the offense tied for its highest success rate of the season. Second, Cousins averaged the fewest yards to go on third down of the Vikings' starting passers. Facing the Packers might've been an easier task with Cousins under duress on just 23.1% of his third-down dropbacks, but 58.1% of his attempts turned into a new series. And, unsurprisingly, most of those throws went to No. 18.

The Kirk Cousins To Justin Jefferson Connection Is Officially Back.

Their First Completion Together Since The 2023 Season.

Just Like Old Times In Minnesota. pic.twitter.com/saEx5XaIVh

— SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) November 15, 2026

It's less about the fact that Justin Jefferson secured 43.3% of the targets. Remember, both T.J. Hockenson and Jordan Addison were out for the game. The quality of Jefferson's workload is what should be our focus. His catchable target rate was above 70% for the first time in over a month. His screen rate was at a season-high (8.6%), along with how often Cousins targeted him on in-breaking routes (46.2%). The only thing we didn't see was a deep completion.

San Francisco did just let CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens get loose for a couple of downfield shots. If there were any time to test that part of the Cousins-Jefferson connection, it'd be in a must-win game against the 49ers.

Downs to business

I want to poke at an idea about Patrick Mahomes real quick. 

"Mahomes hasn't been a great downfield passer since Tyreek Hill left Kansas City."

I've seen similar statements or sentiments about Mahomes over the last few years. And I'm sure I've fallen victim to the same short-sightedness. Because, on its own, the above assertion places the bulk of the talent on the receiver. To be clear, Hill, at his prime, was a demon in cleats. But just as we layer praise onto Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, commending Burrow should come right after. And, sure, there is a Hill-sized hole in the offense. However, let's be honest — the Chiefs have done a poor job of filling it.

  • Rashee Rice: 37th (First Downs per Route Run), 40th (ESPN Open Score)

  • Xavier Worthy: 58th, 67th 

I wanted to highlight these metrics because, forget about creating explosives. Let's just focus on the basics of the receiver position. Can you create separation? Can you keep the offense moving? Neither of Mahomes' primary targets can say yes to either question. Eagles WR Dontayvion Wicks (16) has generated more first downs than Xavier Worthy (15); he hasn't played since Week 6. Bucs WR Chris Godwin Jr. (4.1 yards) creates more separation than Rashee Rice (4.0). I was of the mindset that a big-bodied X-receiver would be a larger boost to the offense. But after thinking through it and watching Sunday's game, I see the vision.

More to come. Here's every @joshdowns reception in his first Chiefs game‼️ pic.twitter.com/qVGKk2sSQk

— Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) November 17, 2026

Eight routes. That's all we got out of Josh Downs against the Falcons. But that didn't matter to Mahomes. The former Colt ended the day with a 62.5% TPRR rate. And there wasn't any hesitation about where the two-time MVP was going with the ball. Four of Downs' five targets came in 2.6 seconds or less (in-rhythm throws). And the fifth? With Mahomes under pressure, he found his new receiver on a back-shoulder fade to the end zone. Even on a light-duty day, you can see Downs taking over Worthy's snaps and Cyrus Allen operating as the deep option by the end of the season. But, more importantly, the uptick in efficient and explosive passing allowed Kansas City to maintain its reliance on its rushing attack. 

💥 28 touches
💥 171 total yards
💥 2 rec TD

Emmett Johnson, the 2025 @bigten RBOY, starred in the @Chiefs' win at Atlanta 🤩@NFL Sunday Ticket On YouTube https://t.co/opRr9OqFQypic.twitter.com/uiKFPxdYAC

— Big Ten Football (@B1Gfootball) November 15, 2026

Despite Mahomes' gaudy numbers, Atlanta still pressured him on 55.3% of his dropbacks, limiting him to his third-lowest passing success rate of the season (41.7%). But it didn't matter when rookie Emmett Johnson could add the complementary component necessary to keep the offense on schedule.

Johnson had a 45.0% early-down rushing success rate, which was greater than three of Kenneth Walker III's eight starts. At 4.23 adjusted yards after contact per attempt, the Chiefs now have four games with a rusher over 4.0 (second-most of any offense). Johnson also added 70 receiving yards.

The bump in passing efficiency led to Johnson seeing the third-lowest stacked box rate of any Chiefs' RB this season (36.4%). Plus, Mahomes continued to target his RBs on at least 20.0% of his throws for the fourth time out of his last five games.

Walker will, and should, resume his RB1 role assuming he's back in Week 11. But against the Cardinals, in a likely blowout scenario, Johnson is a prime flex candidate for this weekend.

Keenan Allen: Has hands, will travel

Back in Week 6, I was trying to understand the makeup of the Colts offense. Yes, my head hurt afterward. But my biggest takeaway was how critical Keenan Allen was to the operation. Daniel Jones had two younger options in Josh Downs and Tyler Warren (literally) right in front of him. And yet, the 34-year-old receiver was responsible for most of Indianapolis' receiving first downs. The trend continued after his move to San Francisco.

Keenan Allen With An 8-Yard Catch For The 49ers First Down.

Still Moving The Chains Like He Always Has.

That's Five Catches For 61 Yards Today.

The Vet Is Looking Real Good Out There. pic.twitter.com/mNHwRfdHwb

— SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) November 15, 2026

Allen couldn't have asked to join the 49ers at a better time. The Cowboys offense pushed Brock Purdy to his third-most dropbacks in a single game this season. Accordingly, he reset his career-high in passing yards (with most of those going to Christian McCaffrey). And amidst the chaos, Allen quickly resumed his role as a target siphon.

  • Target Share: 25.0%, 2nd (among all SF pass-catchers)

  • Targets per Route Run: 33.3%, 1st 

  • Yards per Route Run: 2.90, 2nd 

To be fair, Jacob Cowing and Demarcus Robinson have had time to find their place within the offense. Deebo Samuel Sr. made an immediate impact in his return, turning six touches into 109 total yards and two touchdowns, but Mike Evans' continued absence leaves volume up for grabs. In short, Allen was walking into a viable workload. However, the total amount of targets isn't the only aspect of his first day on the job that has me stashing him on a few benches.

As the above clip highlights, Purdy was already using Allen as an outlet when pressured. The veteran receiver led the team in targets when his QB was under duress. On third downs, Allen was at the top of the totem pole again. McCaffrey was the only other pass-catcher to match Allen in looks. But, as expected, McCaffrey picked up just a few more yards. In addition, he was on the field as much as the rest of the starters in the red zone (71.4% snap rate)

San Francisco won't face another secondary as forgiving as the Cowboys' until Week 13. So, I'd expect the output to dip. However, with this type of usage, Allen should have flex appeal in PPR leagues if you're short on WR options.

Brissett lets it fly in Baltimore

I was trying to keep the context of Kirk Cousins' first game with Minnesota in mind while watching Jacoby Brissett on MNF. Sure, Brissett got four days of practice, compared to Cousins' two. But learning a new system and route timings takes, well, time. Regardless, despite the loss, I'd look at the trade as a success for fantasy managers. 

TruMedia credited Brissett with 50 dropbacks against the Chargers. That's the most of any Ravens QB this season. In fact, that's more than all but five games of the Lamar Jackson era. Baltimore's PROE hit +6.8%, another season-high. And at a +3.0% completion rate over expected, you could see why we liked him as a stabilizing force in Arizona for the fantasy values of Michael Wilson and Trey McBride. However, Brissett didn't concentrate his throws on a couple of receivers as he did for the Cardinals. 

  • Ja'Kobi Lane: 23.4% (Target Rate), 58.4% (Air Yard Share)

  • Mark Andrews: 17.0%, 15.8%

  • Justice Hill: 14.9%, -2.6%

  • Zay Flowers: 14.9%, 9.0%

I'm willing to look at Justice Hill's involvement as a function of the game script. Since Baltimore was trailing for most of the game, Hill played on 45.5% of the snaps. However, the larger concern is Zay Flowers. After starting the season as an intermediate threat (11.5 air yards per target), he was back to a "gadget-like" role, with four of his seven targets near or behind the LOS. Of course, we'll take manufactured touches. They're a signal of intent to keep a key player involved in the offense. If the usage drop, fumble and disparity of a lost season for the Ravens opens up a buy-low window on Flowers, take it. But I'm not so sure the targets to the TEs and RBs will stop.

  • Pressure Rate: 44.0% (Brissett), 40.5% (Jackson), 40.0% (Fagnano), 34.9% (Huntley)

  • Quick Pressure Rate: 40.9%, 44.4%, 75.0%, 59.1%

If you're looking for the reason why Derrick Henry hasn't cracked 60 rushing yards since early October, check out the guys in front of him. The Chargers met Henry at or behind the LOS on 80.0% of his carries. Similarly, Baltimore's protection has forced its QBs to make faster decisions (i.e., throw to the short-area options). We'll still get intermediate shots to the WRs, but because of the offensive line issues, expect to see the opportunities spread out for the rest of the season.

item.title: Fantasy football injury report: Week 11 updates on Walker, Bowers
item.description: Could the Chiefs give star RB Kenneth Walker another week to rest his groin? What progress is Raiders TE Brock Bowers making?
item.content:encoded:
The standard bumps and bruises that fantasy football managers must deal with every week are compounded by six NFL teams going on bye in Week 11. The status of two key performers − Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker and Raiders tight end Brock Bowers − could be the difference between winning a losing.

So let's turn our attention to some of the most prominent players' ongoing injury issues that will impact fantasy managers most in Week 11. As always, keep an eye on the latest developments leading up to kickoff with our player notes page.

ON BYE: Atlanta, Cleveland, Green Bay, L.A. Rams, New England, Seattle

WEEK 11 RANKINGS:QB | RB | WR | TE | K | DST | FLEX

RB Kenneth Walker III, Kansas City Chiefs

The biggest injury question of Week 11 revolves around Walker and his groin injury. The Chiefs should feel pretty confident that Emmett Johnson can handle another week of filling in for Walker after he piled up 171 total yards and scored a pair of touchdowns against the Falcons. It's entirely possible the Chiefs will err on the side of caution with their star. If so, Johnson could once again be a top-5 running back option.

QB Baker Mayfield, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Mayfield has shown throughout his career that he will try to play through just about any injury. The next few days might put his resolve to the test. The veteran suffered a foot injury late in Week 9's game against the Bears, and he's been wearing a walking boot through the Bucs bye week. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport suggests Mayfield "seems to be trending" toward sitting out Sunday vs. the Lions, but we can't rule Baker out just yet. Rookie Jalon Daniels would be in line to start if Mayfield can't go.

QB Geno Smith, New York Jets

Smith left Sunday's game twice with two different injuries: one to his head and the other to his ankle. He did get checked out for a possible concussion in the second quarter and was cleared to return to the game, but then tweaked his ankle in the second half and did not come back. Coach Aaron Glenn said Monday that Smith would start this Sunday against the Chargers if healthy.

RB David Montgomery, Houston Texans

Montgomery has missed the Texans' last four games with a groin injury, but he's expected to return for this Thursday's clash with the Colts. It's good timing for Houston after Woody Marks entering the concussion protocol after Sunday's game and being unlikely to be cleared over the short week. Montgomery practiced in full on Monday and Tuesday, but be careful going all-in on him in his return. He hasn't rushed for more than 33 yards in any game since totaling 60 and a pair of touchdowns in the season opener.

RB Kyle Monangai, Chicago Bears

Monangai (toe/thumb) has missed five consecutive games and is coming off a bye week. He returned to the field in pads during unofficial practices on Monday and Tuesday, so things are looking positive heading into a Week 11 matchup against the Saints − who've given up the second-most fantasy points per game this season to running backs.

WR DeVonta Smith, Philadelphia Eagles

Coming off the Eagles' bye, Smith will have an extra week of rest for his troublesome hamstring injury that caused him to miss five of the last six games. He won't have QB Jalen Hurts throwing to him regardless, which will cause his fantasy value to take a hit whenever he returns. Joe Milton is expected to start at quarterback this week against Pittsburgh.

WR Mike Evans, San Francisco 49ers

The Niners have had trouble keeping wide receivers healthy all season, but they could be close to full strength on Sunday if Evans is good to go. The veteran has missed the last three games with an Achilles injury but coach Kyle Shanahan seems optimistic Evans can suit up for Sunday's matchup against the Vikings in Mexico City.

TE Brock Bowers, Las Vegas Raiders

Bowers left Sunday's game early with an ankle injury and is considered day-to-day entering the new week. Coach Klint Kubiak told reporters it's "not as bad as we thought, but it's still a significant injury." That doesn't sound promising as the Raiders head to Denver on Sunday. Michael Mayer would be in line for more targets if Bowers isn't at full strength.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Fantasy football injury report: Week 11 updates on Walker, Bowers

item.title: Third time’s a charm; Dolphins sign new kicker to replace Zane Gonzalez
item.description: Dolphins sign kicker Daniel Carlson to team’s practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, the Miami Dolphins worked out two kickers amidst Zane Gonzalez’s struggles regarding the conversion of field goal attempts — a pretty important task for kickers in the National Football League. Despite impressive days from Ben Sauls and Daniel Carlson, Miami decided to roll with Gonzalez last Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts. That decision came back to bite them in the tuchus… big time.

In a game in which the Dolphins lost by just two points, Gonzalez missed two field goals and an extra point try. Those gaffes cost the team the game, and the kicker his job in Miami, leaving general manager, Jon-Eric Sullivan, to go searching for his third player at the position during the 2026 NFL season.

On Tuesday, the Dolphins signed Carlson to their practice squad — giving the team roster flexibility while being able to call up the kicker to their active roster on game days three times before being required to sign him to their 53-man squad.

Carlson — a 9-year veteran — has played for a number of teams in his career. His most recent stint was with the New Orleans Saints. However, Carlson was released earlier this season after going just 8 for 12 on field goal tries in 7 games played. For his entire career, Carlson has made 233 tries on 271 attempts — good for an 86% average. For the sake of comparison, Gonzalez has a career field-goal conversion rate of 79.6%.

Our first opportunity to find out if Sullivan has finally found his kicker will take place when the Dolphins travel to Highmark Stadium this Sunday to take on the Buffalo Bills.

item.title: What Are the Chances of the Vikings Getting “Flexed” the Rest of This Season?
item.description: Let’s take a look
item.content:encoded:
Now that we’re into the second half of the 2026 NFL season, the potential for games to get “flexed” into different time slots has increased. Yesterday, as there were rumors that the Week 12 matchup between the Minnesota Vikings and the Atlanta Falcons at U.S. Bank Stadium might get flexed to Sunday Night Football that week, the league decided to move the game between the Las Vegas Raiders and Cleveland Browns to that spot instead.

You read that correctly. . .the league moved a game between Cleveland and Las Vegas into a prime time spot, moving a game between the Los Angeles Chargers and New England Patriots out of that spot.

So, with Week 12 no longer a possibility, do the Vikings have any other potential chances of being moved into a prime time slot for the rest of the season? Let’s take a look.

To briefly review the flex scheduling rules, games can be flexed to Sunday Night Football with 12 days notice between Weeks 11-13 and with 6 days notice between Weeks 14-17, to Monday Night Football with 12 days notice between Weeks 12-17, and to Thursday Night Football with 21 days notice between Weeks 13-17. Basically, time is running short for the league to move games around, particularly if they want to move them to Thursday night. With that, here we go.

Week 13: Panthers at Vikings, currently scheduled for 3:25 PM Central on CBS

Sunday Night Football: Texans at Steelers

Monday Night Football: Cowboys at Seahawks

If the league is going to move this matchup into one of those two prime time spots, we’re going to know by this time next week, as it’s the last week that requires 12 days notice before moving a game into either of those spots. (The Sunday night requirement drops to 6 days starting in Week 14, as outlined above.) On top of that, the league has a couple of other matchups they’d likely find more attractive than Panthers/Vikings, such as Jaguars/Bears and Bengals/Browns, depending on which matchups the networks are protecting.

Week 14: Vikings at Patriots, currently scheduled for Thursday Night Football

Sunday Night Football: Bills at Packers

Monday Night Football: Steelers at Jaguars

The league would have to make the decision by tomorrow if they wanted to move Vikings/Patriots off of Thursday Night Football because of the 21-day notice requirement. The issue there is that two of the most potentially attractive matchups are already in prime time slots for that week. Chiefs/Bengals and Rams/49ers are both set for the late window on FOX in Week 14, and I don’t know if FOX can protect both of those games or not. If they can’t, one of those could be a possibility. Again, if it’s going to happen, we’ll know by tomorrow.

Week 15: Lions at Vikings, currently scheduled for Sunday Night Football

Yeah, the league isn’t moving this one.

Week 16: Commanders at Vikings, date and time currently TBD

Thursday Night Football: Texans at Eagles

Sunday Night Football: Jaguars at Cowboys

Monday Night Football: Giants at Lions

Week 16 could get a little tricky. Vikings/Commanders is one of four games (along with Buccaneers/Falcons, Bengals/Colts, and Panthers/Steelers) that is currently set to, potentially, be a part of a Saturday doubleheader on the NFL Network. The two games from that group that aren’t selected for that Saturday, according to the footnote on the NFL’s schedule page for Week 16, are eligible to be played on Thursday night. . .or on Sunday afternoon. . .or on Sunday night. . .or on Monday night. It’s Thunderdome out there in Week 16, kids. If both the Texans and Eagles continue to struggle, that Thursday night matchup might be one the league is looking to move off of for a prime time spot. But whether or not they move that Vikings/Patriots game out of the Week 14 spot could play a role in that, too.

Lot of ins, lot of outs. . .lot of strands to keep in the dude’s head. The Week 16 matchups are supposed to be determined “immediately after Week 14,” so we’ll see how that works out.

Week 17: Vikings at Jets, currently scheduled for noon Central on CBS

Thursday Night Football: Ravens at Bengals

Sunday Night Football: Eagles at Niners

Monday Night Football: Texans at Packers

I’m not going to spend a whole lot of time on this one. I just don’t think the league is going to put Vikings/Jets into a prime time spot for any reason, honestly.

Week 18: Bears at Vikings, TBD

As the league has done for the last few years, the schedule for Week 18 won’t be known until Week 17 is pretty much completely in the books and we know which matchups are going to carry the greatest playoff implications/drama going into the final week of the season.

So, should we worry about the Vikings potentially getting their schedule changed over the second half of the season? It doesn’t look like it, honestly, but the league could give us a surprise. The biggest surprise would be moving the New England game off of Thursday Night, but if that’s going to happen, we’ll know about it by tomorrow because of the timing requirements.
