item.title: Grading the Browns offense during their midseason bye week
item.description: A unit that has had its struggles, grading the Cleveland Browns offense during their Week 1 bye week.
item.content:encoded:
Describing the Cleveland Browns offense from last season is easy; to sum it up, it was abysmal. Top to bottom. From the offensive line, quarterback, skill positions, everything was bad. GM Andrew Berry spent the entire offseason rebuilding the entire unit. With the team entering their bye week, we will give a grade to the 2026 Browns offense that was created out of all those moves.

Browns roster, offense: What has changed?

Everything.

Last year, Cleveland’s offense was towards the bottom in every statistical category. Despite the young pieces with running backs Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson, tight end Harold Fannin Jr and a reliable veteran wide receiver, Jerry Jeudy, it didn’t have much success overall. The offensive line was older and less effective, and the quarterback play was below average.

Berry spent the entire offseason rebuilding this offense.

  • Fired head coach Kevin Stefanski; hired Todd Monken
  • Traded for right tackle Tytus Howard, signed left guard Zion Johnson, center/guard Elgton Jenkins, drafted rookie left tackle Spencer Fano and right guard Austin Barber
  • Drafted rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston

It was a lot of work, but Berry did what was necessary to improve one of the worst offenses in the league last season. Comparing the numbers from last year’s offense at the bye week to this year’s offense, you can see a stark difference, even if it still ranks in the bottom half of the league:

Browns Offense pre-bye (last season)

  • 31st in offensive EPA per play
  • 32nd in offensive success rate
  • 32nd in Dropback EPA/per play
  • 13th in Offensive Rush EPA per play
  • 32nd in Dropback Success Rate
  • 31st in Rush success rate

Browns offense pre-bye (2026 season)

  • 23rd in EPA per play
  • 23rd in Offensive Success Rate
  • 22nd in Dropback EPA/per play
  • 27th in Rush EPA/per play
  • 20th in Dropback Success Rate
  • 21st in total offense
  • 23rd in Rush Success Rate

Having better offensive personnel has something to do with the numbers looking better, but it is a night-and-day difference from last season. The one thing that the team lacked last season was generating explosive plays in the passing game, rookies Concepcion and Boston have changed that. Fannin has also been a part of a somewhat revitalized passing game, giving Cleveland something with those three in the skill position room.

The one thing that the team has lacked for years is competent quarterback play. Going into the season, the Browns quarterback room was considered a major weakness. Granted, it still is because there is no long-term solution on the roster, but the room has some form of stability from an unlikely individual.

Going back to the offseason, many believed that second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders would be the starter for the entire season. However, quarterback Deshaun Watson took the job despite his tenure in Cleveland not being what he envisioned. Many believed that Watson was done after how he lashed out at the fanbase after the second preseason game in which he was booed.

Fast forward to now, Watson is playing better than he did in 2024. Head coach Todd Monken has something to do with that:

Monken had an honest conversation with Watson, and it appears to have benefited the quarterback, and his play looks different than before. Playing with more confidence, better pocket presence, utilizing his legs, and showing signs of how he looked in Houston. Granted, Watson hasn’t been perfect, but the Browns have lacked competent QB play last year, and Watson is giving the team that now.

In terms of the offensive line, the unit has been better than expected. Fano has been sensational. The same can be said for Barber. Johnson, whom Cleveland paid in free agency, has been better than people give him credit for. Jenkins and Howard have been the subject of criticism (unfair at times), but they are providing stability at their respective positions.

What needs to improve?

Two things come to mind:

The running game hasn’t materialized this season. At times, it feels as if the running game is coming along until it reaches a roadblock. It could improve after the bye week or possibly next season. For the running game to work effectively, the offensive line has to be better, and the backs have to improve as well. Whether it’s opening up rushing lanes consistently or the running back having better vision, the running has to get better.

The second thing is the slow starts, which have also been a common theme. It’s more of a recurring theme. The offense simply has to get out of the gate faster and not wait until the game is out of reach to start executing. Going no-huddle or tempo could be easy fixes, but the slow starts offensively have to stop.

Grade

Overall, the Browns offense has flaws, but this is a unit that is 10x better than last season. Competent QB play, quality talent at the skill positions, a competent offensive line, and a good offensive coordinator are all Cleveland needed. The QB position isn’t solved long-term, but overall this unit is competent and has made massive improvements from last year.

Grade: C-, maybe a C

How would you grade the Browns offense going into their bye week?

The last two weeks in the NFL have seen favorites dominate the betting card, going 23-6 straight up and 19-10 against the spread. Both the hit rates far exceed the standard implied probability of the odds, which means bettors backing the favorites have been on cruise control. This usually means bad news for the bookmakers, as most often bettors put money-line favorites into parlays. The rates of cashing those parlays far exceeds the hold of the market bought into or the price paid out. I won't forecast if this will continue or not, but I do think it slightly impacts the pricing of the games this week.

The way that I foresee the recent results impacting the Week 11 lines is that favorites have inflated prices relative to a standard market or power rating system. If we use the Week 10 closing lines, with an adjustment for the actual outcome differential from the pre-game spread, we would see only three double-digit favorites this week; instead, we currently have five. And most of them are inflated against my numbers.

They include:

  • Houston Texans (-12) vs. Indianapolis Colts; I would make it -9.5.

  • Chicago Bears (-11.5) vs. New Orleans Saints; I would make it -9.5.

  • Kansas City Chiefs (-16) vs. Arizona Cardinals: I would make it -15.

  • Buffalo Bills (-16.5) vs. Miami Dolphins: I would make it -15.5.

  • Denver Broncos (-10) vs. Las Vegas Raiders; I would make it -10.

If you like any of the underdogs here, my numbers would support a play on them against the spread. There is still one favorite I see value on, though.

Jacksonville Jaguars (-6, 46.5) at New York Giants

The Jaguars have been demolishing teams this season. They are 7-2, leading the AFC South by four games and have a net point differential of +125. For context, that is the biggest point differential through nine games since the 2021 Buffalo Bills were +145. The Jaguars are averaging a +13.9 scoring margin per game.

Not only have they been crushing opponents, but the Jaguars this week will be the best version of themselves this season because of the additions at the trade deadline of defensive tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III. These acquisitions were made prior to last week's game but neither player suited up against the Tennessee Titans — the Jaguars covered the 10.5-point closing line on the road, winning by 17.

They are healthy, well coached, strong on both sides of the ball and still only a 6-point favorite on the road against the New York Giants. The Giants have overperformed expectations and maybe won a few games they didn't deserve to. I expect a regression to the mean for New York, and Jacksonville to stay so far in front of the pack it's hard to catch up. Jaguars -6 could close at -7.5 by Sunday.

Bet: Jaguars -6

New Orleans Saints at Chicago Bears (-11.5, 49)

I look forward to seeing the offensive plays Ben Johnson draws up after a bye week and at home playing the lowly Saints defense. The Bears offense ranks top 10 in every important stat: points per game, yards per game, third down conversion rate, explosive play rate, success rate, EPA per play and drives that result in a score. I am not sure if the prop exists, but something I will look for is Bears to score on their first drive, both yes and yes to a touchdown.

While the Saints have struggled this season, it's not due to offensive woes. They are seventh in third-down conversion rate and top five in red zone efficiency and quarterback completion rate. Their head coach Kellen Moore employs a system that prioritizes pace and fast play calls, so this is a game where both offenses should produce points and I am looking for an over.

It's always a bit gutsy to back an early-week over in a November game being played at Soldier Field in Chicago. Cold weather, rain and wind are all cause for concern. Looking at the 10-day forecast, I am seeing 20-25% chance of precipitation, no strong winds and a 50-degree temperature on gameday. With these conditions and these offenses, I want the over 49 thinking this can close above 50.

Bet: Over 49
